events.title: I was awarded $1 million in scholarships to NYU. I also sacrificed a lot of my teenage life to get there.
events.summary: The author received more than $1 million in combined scholarship offers from over 20 colleges before attending NYU. Courtesy of Omarion Calloway I was offered more than $1 million in scholarships from over 20 colleges. I spent hours every night searching for scholarships and financial aid. I ultimately earned a full ride to NYU, but getting there was a job in itself. When I was 18, local headlines and social media posts about me all focused on the exact same number: I was accepted into more than 20 colleges and offered over $1 million in combined scholarship funding. I'm sure that to people reading the news, that seven-figure total sounded like a lottery win . What the headlines missed was the invisible labor it took to get there. People saw the final funding amount. They didn't see the unpaid late-night hours I worked every single night, completely on my own, just to afford my future. No manual, no guidance counselor, and no road map I grew up in Montgomery, Alabama, determined to become the first person in my family to graduate from college. My goal was to study film and television at New York University. Getting accepted was one hurdle, but figuring out how to pay for it was the real wall. My family did not have extra money for tuition , and my mom had never navigated higher education. When I asked for help at school, my guidance counselor had no answers for an out-of-state dream. On top of that, I was trying to figure this out during the COVID-19 pandemic, isolated at home and staring at confusing college portals, financial aid pages, and scholarship search engines I had never seen before. The author with his mother during the COVID-19 pandemic. Courtesy of Omarion Calloway Nobody explained how to navigate the Common App, the single online application platform that allows students to apply to hundreds of different colleges at once. Nobody showed me how to find legitimate scholarship databases or how to request application fee waivers, so I wouldn't go broke just applying. Having internet access gave me a starting point, but it didn't give me a map. I realized early on that if I didn't hunt down the answers myself, nobody was going to hand them to me. Working the late shift at home High school schedules are already full. My days consisted of seven hours of school followed by homework. After that came my responsibilities at home: since age 10, I had been helping care for my grandmother and my disabled uncle while my mom worked two jobs to pay our bills. Between classes, schoolwork, and family caretaking, my daily bandwidth was entirely tapped out. But I couldn't afford to wait for a miracle. Starting in my junior year and carrying straight through senior year, my second shift began the moment my family went to sleep. From 11 p.m. to 3 a.m., I managed college portals, tracked deadlines on spreadsheets, searched for scholarships, and drafted essay after essay. The author received a scholarship from the Continental Societies, Inc. in 2022. Courtesy of Omarion Calloway The process behind the funding The hardest part wasn't keeping track of dates on a spreadsheet. It was learning how to write about myself for an audience while building a strategy from scratch. Because I was applying mostly out-of-state, I couldn't rely on local state grants. Instead, I had to secure the maximum federal financial aid I could through the FAFSA, hunt down fee waivers to eliminate costs across more than 20 colleges, scour online databases for independent corporate grants, and apply directly to universities for institutional merit and need-based packages. I spent hours tailoring my story to different prompts, explaining to review committees who I was, what my life was like at home, and why my experiences mattered. Doing that over and over was exhausting, especially when my 15-hour effort sometimes ended in rejection or, worse, total silence. But because I needed options, I had to brush it off, log back in, and apply to the next opportunity. The hidden cost When college admissions became a second job, my life stopped being about learning and growing. It became about performing and surviving. Balancing school, caregiving, and hours of nightly application work left zero room for rest. It triggered chronic stress, sleep deprivation, and the constant fear that I wasn't doing enough. I completely missed out on the typical high school experience . While most of my classmates went to football games, hung out on weekends, and enjoyed their senior year milestones, my world looked very different. I had one close friend in high school who was also helping care for her grandmother. The author with his best friend at their middle school prom. Courtesy of Omarion Calloway Outside of our shared understanding of what it meant to have real responsibilities at home, I was glued to my computer screen . Every spare hour that wasn't spent on family care was sacrificed to finish another essay or track down another deadline. The process also stripped away my authentic voice. To win aid, you're asked to package your lived experiences into a polished pitch. Sitting at a screen at 2 a.m., unpacking my family's financial struggles for committees of strangers, forced me to sound older and more corporate than I actually was. The outcome and what came after After dozens of applications and months of late nights, the work paid off. The cumulative value of the financial aid and scholarship offers I received across those 20-plus acceptance letters passed $1 million, and I ultimately accepted a full ride to NYU. The author with his mother after being accepted to NYU. Courtesy of Omarion Calloway When my mom saw the official financial aid package, she cried in relief. For the public, that million-dollar stat made a great headline. For my family, it meant I could attend the school I chose without taking on crushing debt. I graduated from NYU in 2026 with my degree in film and television. Looking back, that experience taught me how to navigate complex systems and advocate for myself when no road map existed. The author graduated from NYU in 2026. Courtesy of Omarion Calloway We talk a lot about the American dream, the idea that hard work opens every door. But my experience has shown that the playing field isn't level from the start. For students without wealth, getting good grades is only half the battle. The other half is surviving an exhausting second job just to pay for the chance to compete. I reached my goal, but no 18-year-old should have to work an unpaid graveyard shift every night just to earn a seat at the table. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Microsoft brings AI-ready capabilities across its India cloud infrastructure
events.summary: AI ambition into action: Microsoft brings AI-ready capabilities across its India cloud infrastructure, establishes India South Central region as a strategic hub for Asia and Global South India South Central, Microsoft’s new Hyderabad datacenter region, brings AI-ready infrastructure and a resilient three-zone architecture designed to scale with demand, as Azure and AI capabilities deepen progressively over time. Microsoft’s India cloud regions provide capabilities aligned with MeitY guidelines to help customers address applicable data protection, cybersecurity, and sector-specific requirements, including India’s DPDP framework and guidance from RBI and CERT-In. High-efficiency mechanical cooling delivers effectively zero water use for cooling, supporting more responsible AI infrastructure. Microsoft equips more than 10 million Indians with AI skills towards its commitment of skilling 20 million people by 2030 As the company with the largest hyperscaler cloud presence in the country, Microsoft’s AI infrastructure is contributing to India’s datacenter economy flywheel, which is estimated to generate $140-200B economic output through 2030, as per a BCG study NEW DELHI, September 21, 2026 — At the Microsoft AI Infrastructure Summit, the company today outlined how it is turning India’s frontier AI ambition into capability at scale. Microsoft announced that India South Central, its new Hyderabad datacenter region, has been designated a strategic hub for Asia and the Global South, reflecting its long-term commitment to capacity expansion, resilience and AI innovation in the region. Puneet Chandok, President, Microsoft India and South Asia, also announced in his keynote address that Microsoft’s datacenter regions across India are now AI-enabled, built with AI-capable hardware, high-efficiency cooling systems and the platform foundation required to host and run advanced AI workloads, bringing frontier AI capability closer to Indian organizations. The now-live India South Central datacenter region in Hyderabad features a resilient three-zone architecture designed for sustained expansion, with additional Azure and AI services planned for the region. As supported services become available, organizations will be able to deploy eligible sensitive workloads in India using controls designed to support their security, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Microsoft’s latest datacenter region in India marks a significant step in its US$20.5 billion commitment to the country, turning that investment into operational infrastructure for India’s cloud and AI future. Leading enterprises and critical infrastructure organizations, such as Adani Group, Bajaj Finserv, HDFC Bank and PB Pay, have already signed up on the new region. A BCG study estimates that the datacenter buildout in India could catalyze wider economic flywheel and generate $140-200B economic output for India through 2030. With India’s largest hyperscale cloud presence in the country, Microsoft’s investments continue to meaningfully contribute to the country’s expanding economic growth. Speaking at the event, Shri Jitin Prasada, Hon’ble Minister of State for Commerce and Industry, and Electronics & Information Technology , said, “India’s ambition is to be an AI-first nation. The launch of Microsoft’s India South Central datacenter region strengthens the digital infrastructure needed to support that ambition. As we advance the IndiaAI Mission, investments such as these expand national AI capability, accelerate innovation, and enable developers, enterprises, and public institutions to build and deploy AI with confidence. With its talent, entrepreneurial energy, and digital public infrastructure, India is well-positioned to lead AI adoption at scale and contribute innovations that benefit people in India and around the world.” Puneet Chandok, President, Microsoft India and South Asia , said , “ India heard our commitment. Today, India can see it — built, live and running. India South Central is our fourth cloud region in the country, built for advanced AI workloads and a strategic hub for Asia and the Global South. It is where our $20.5 billion investment becomes operational infrastructure, with leading Indian enterprises already running on it. But compute alone does not make a nation AI-ready. Capability does — the ability to take AI from pilot to production on platforms that are sovereign-ready, secure and sustainable, in a region cooled with effectively zero water. That is why we have already equipped more than 10 million Indians with AI skills, on the way to 20 million by 2030. India has the talent and the ambition. Now it has the infrastructure to build the next generation of Frontier Firms — and we are building alongside it. “ Message from Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft India South Central region launches with a broad portfolio of Azure services and is designed to support the full portfolio of Azure and AI services, including Microsoft Foundry, as additional capabilities roll out in the coming months . The ‘strategic hub’ ambition extends beyond serving domestic demand. India brings together hyperscale infrastructure, engineering talent, a fast-growing digital economy and experience building technology for complex, diverse markets. This combination can support customers across South Asia, accelerate innovation for Asia and create solutions relevant to the Global South. Beyond AI-ready datacenters, Microsoft is also investing in the critical digital infrastructure that enables AI at scale. As a consortium partner in the planned India-Southeast Asia (I-2SEA) submarine cable system, Microsoft is supporting the development of a 3,600-kilometre subsea corridor linking India, Malaysia and Singapore. With dual landings in India, at Machilipatnam and South Chennai, the system will strengthen regional connectivity, improve network resilience, and provide the high-capacity foundation needed to support growing AI, cloud and hyperscale demand across India and the region. The cable system is targeted to be ready for service in 2029. Beyond investing in infrastructure, Microsoft announced another milestone in its AI commitment to India. Microsoft Elevate India has equipped more than 10 million Indians with AI skills towards its commitment to skilling 20 million people by 2030. About 25 percent of the learners have progressed beyond foundational AI course and gained credentials for additional learning pathways. This progress provides strong momentum to India’s national skilling ambition, set out by Hon’ble Prime Minister Narendra Modi, to build a new generation of frontier professionals ready to participate in and lead the AI economy. Microsoft continues to invest in India’s digital future through its Data Center Academy , which prepares students for careers in the rapidly growing datacenter industry.

events.title: Ceuta solidarity shirt row: How the crisis engulfed Spanish football
events.summary: Football has been dragged into growing tensions over the influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Madrid, Spain – Thirteen minutes into La Liga’s Madrid derby on Sunday, a banner was unfurled in the Metropolitano Stadium’s south stand stating: “Ceuta es Espana. Ni se arruga, ni se tapa.” (Ceuta is Spain. It is neither rolled up, nor covered.) It was a reference to the controversy involving Real Madrid players Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate, who in a previous football match against Elche had rolled-up shirts carrying a solidarity message linked to Ceuta, the Spanish enclave at the centre of growing political tensions between Spain and Morocco over the influx of migrants and refugees. list 1 of 4 Kyrie Irving will ‘take care’ of Al-Shaair’s NFL fine on Hind Rajab message list 2 of 4 Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal says he has experienced racism ‘a thousand times’ list 3 of 4 Eala and Pathirage headline top athletes to watch at the 2026 Asian Games list 4 of 4 VAR error admitted in Haaland goal, but will referees be held accountable? A record 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco to Ceuta over the course of two days in late July, overwhelming local resources and creating a humanitarian crisis. The Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras documented 141 deaths across both sides of the border in the immediate aftermath. Mbappe and Konate have strong ties to the African continent. Konate was born and raised in Paris by parents who migrated from Mali, while France captain Mbappe grew up in Bondy, outside Paris, to parents who came from Cameroon and Algeria. Mbappe said his gesture did not reflect a lack of support for Ceuta. “I also wanted to think about all the people who are suffering, because in the end I am human and I don’t want to prioritise the suffering of one group over another,” he said. He also said he wanted to acknowledge migrants who had suffered or lost their lives during the crisis. Real Madrid later said it respected each player’s freedom to participate in the initiative. A day earlier, Barcelona had chosen not to wear the shirts before their La Liga game against Levante. La Liga president Javier Tebas, meanwhile, criticised the three Real Madrid players and said he did not regard the campaign as political. David Aganzo, president of Spanish footballers’ union AFE, said players instead needed to be properly informed about what they were being asked to wear and why. While the debate over Spanish football’s support for Ceuta followed Real into their derby against fierce rivals Atletico Madrid on Sunday, it also united supporters from both sides for two minutes as they joined in chants of “Ceuta no se vende, Ceuta se defiende” (Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended) before the usual hostility of the derby resumed. Mbappe and Vinicius were also the target of whistles from both sets of fans when Real’s starting XI was announced prior to kickoff. Jorge Garcia, a 32-year-old Atletico Madrid supporter, believed they deserved the jeering. Speaking to Al Jazeera after the match, Garcia termed the players’ move “disrespectful” to both Ceuta and Spain. The campaign was launched on September 11 by Asociacion Valenciana de Empresarios (AVE), a non-profit business association, which described the move as an expression of solidarity with Ceuta’s residents and businesses amid an influx of migrants and a message of “territorial and social cohesion in Spain”. AVE is chaired by businessman Vicente Boluda, a former interim Real Madrid president whose maritime group also operates in Ceuta. Spain coach Luis de la Fuente travelled to Ceuta with the World Cup trophy, declaring: “This is Spain, this is Ceuta.” Real Madrid president Florentino Perez later visited and said the trip had been organised weeks earlier and was not a response to the controversy involving his players. Youssef Temsamani, a Spain-based Moroccan journalist, believes the players found themselves in a difficult position: wearing the shirt could be interpreted as taking a political position, but declining to do so could be portrayed as showing a lack of solidarity. Temsamani said migrants should also form part of discussions about solidarity with Ceuta, and criticised descriptions of the crossings in parts of Spain’s political and media debate as an “invasion” or “occupation”. Luhay Hamido, president of AD Ceuta football club, defended the right of individual players to make their own decisions and said he respected those who wore it and those who did not. “We cannot force anyone to identify with a cause they do not understand,” he told Al Jazeera, suggesting footballers are sometimes simply told to put on a shirt in the tunnel without having received a full explanation. The scale of the crisis that prompted the solidarity campaign remains difficult to quantify precisely.

events.title: X will now tell users when governments have forced it to limit their posts
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt X on Monday announced it will now tell users when their posts have been “shadowbanned,” meaning shown to fewer people, due to the company’s compliance with local laws. The feature is an expansion of the social network’s earlier transparency tool called “Under the Hood,” which allows users to see if any labels have been applied to their account or their posts that could have affected their visibility on the platform. It will also highlight any downranking of users’ posts due to government-required content filtering. We’ve expanded Under The Hood after seeing people’s appreciation of more transparency into government-required content filtering. In addition to showing labels applied to your account and posts in the prior month, Under The Hood now shows if your account or posts had their… https://t.co/Op5rBnE1jg pic.twitter.com/ZUrbkO28ay — X Open Source (@XOpenSource) September 19, 2026 Previously, information about how an X user’s account or posts were being labeled and downranked was not available to end users. As a result, many often accused the company, formerly known as Twitter, of having shadowbanned them. In addition, most companies that share data about government requests do so on an aggregate basis through “transparency reports,” not at the account or post level. That began to change when, in August, X rolled out its transparency tool to offer more visibility into its moderation decisions. The “Under the Hood” option in the X app settings allows anyone who has posted at least 10 times during the month to download their aggregate stats as a JSON file, a standard data format. (Non-technical users can drop the file into any AI chatbot to have it explained.) This same process will now show if an account or posts have had their visibility limited because X is complying with local laws. The file will also include which posts were withheld in a country following a legal demand, and which country made the request. Governments cite a range of reasons for such demands, from laws against hate speech to terrorism-related content to election rules. Of course, critics, including free-expression groups, say some countries also use these laws to squash political dissent. The update follows a number of other transparency-related efforts at X, including the open-sourcing of its “For You” algorithm, which selects the posts in users’ main feed, and an expansion of its efforts to open source parts of its codebase . The latter involved adding more detail, including on the model configuration, filtering, and core ranking system details. That means the code now includes the parameters used to weight different signals — information that is key to understanding which posts are actually displayed. At the time of that open-sourcing effort, X’s vice president of product, Keith Coleman, said it was “the kind of thing that I think people will be fairly shocked that we are releasing.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Paramount Skydance has emerged victorious in its pursuit of a $110bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery after it settled lawsuits with California and 11 other states and a Hollywood writers union that sued to block the deal, paving the way for one of the largest media mergers in history. The settlement, reported on Monday, will include independent editorial boards to oversee CNN and CBS amid concerns that political pressure could sway coverage. The lawsuits were brought by a coalition of 12 state attorneys general . list 1 of 4 Twelve US states sue Paramount to block Warner Bros merger list 2 of 4 US judge orders pause on Paramount–Warner Bros merger list 3 of 4 Paramount Skydance mulls CNN sale amid antitrust merger challenge list 4 of 4 Paramount CEO may remove operations from California over stalled merger But free speech advocates are not convinced that will be helpful. “An independent editorial board for CNN and CBS is a weak half-measure. The fish rots from the head, and this particular fish is headed by a compromised oligarch with a history of throwing journalists under the bus to advance his business interests,” Seth Stern, director of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, told Al Jazeera. “The editorial board actually poses its own First Amendment problems when created pursuant to a settlement with the government. It’s unclear how the attorneys general can constitutionally hold Paramount accountable if the board doesn’t do its job without themselves interfering in content – the exact problem they’re supposedly trying to solve.” Paramount Skydance is owned by tech tycoon Larry Ellison, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The company is run by Ellison’s son, David, raising concerns the relationship could sway coverage of Trump and his policies. The settlements are a major win for David. The settlement also includes a $30m penalty if the media giant fails to produce 30 movies per year as it had promised, according to Reuters news agency. It caps months of regulatory and legal wrangling over a deal that would dramatically concentrate power across Hollywood’s film, TV, streaming and news businesses. By securing concessions aimed at preserving newsroom independence and maintaining movie production, Paramount appears to have addressed some of the concerns, bringing the two companies closer to completing a merger that will create one of the world’s largest media and entertainment groups. Paramount did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. On Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported that there were other considerations, including selling off CNN as well as creating an oversight board to help the cable news giant maintain editorial independence. Apart from the July lawsuit by the coalition of attorneys general, the Writers Guild of America, had also sued to stop the deal. Bloomberg reported on Monday that the Guild had a reached a settlement over the weekend. Terms of the deal will include concessions for workers, Bloomberg said citing an unnamed source. The company also agreed to protections for journalists at CBS and CNN that include headcount requirements for both outlets, it said. The lawsuit represented a hurdle to bringing the two media giants together, a deal the Trump administration had already cleared. Other measures under consideration include selling some cable channels, according to the Wall Street Journal. The settlement will help Paramount avoid a $7m daily fee it owes Warner Bros shareholders for each day the deal does not close after September 30. On Wall Street, both companies’ stocks surged on the news. Paramount Skydance was up 10 percent in midday trading while Warner Bros Discovery jumped 11 percent on Monday.

events.title: Bitcoin hits highest level since January at $86,000, as the market debates whether the 'crypto winter' is over
events.summary: Matt Hougan, CIO at Bitwise, told CNBC the "crypto winter" is over and investors may witness the "strongest and longest-running bull market in crypto's history." The price rise comes even as Senate last week voted to block the Clarity Act, a key piece of legislation, from advancing. Bitcoin rose above $86,000 on Monday as the cryptocurrency continued its sharp rally over the past few days. Bitcoin was trading at $85,863.40, up around 5.8%, according to CoinMetrics. Earlier in the day, the cryptocurrency rose as high as $86,349.90 , its highest level since late Jan. 29. Investors are assessing whether the "crypto winter" — a depressed period of digital asset prices — which began after bitcoin hit an all-time high of over $126,000 in October 2025, is over. "I do think it's over, it's crypto spring, the crocuses are blooming," Matt Hougan, CIO at Bitwise, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday. "I think this will actually be the strongest and longest-running bull market in crypto's history." While bitcoin is still down this year, it has risen more than 8% in the past week and 34% over the past 3 months. It is still well off its record high. Hougan said even though the market was down for a while, the "fundamentals went up" in cryptocurrency, pointing to more transactions across blockchains and involvement from major firms like BlackRock. "So I think we had this unusual situation where you had a cyclical decline in prices even as you had a secular improvement in fundamentals. And now I suspect that prices are going to catch up toward the end of the year," Hougan said. "I don't think if I came back next year, we'd still be below those all-time highs." Analysts at BTIG said in a note on Sunday that, as long as the $75,000 level of bitcoin holds, "bulls can target a push through 82k on the way to" $90,000. Crypto-related stocks, including Strategy and Coinbase , were higher in U.S. trading on Monday. The rally comes even as the U.S. Senate last week blocked the Clarity Act from advancing. It would have set up a framework for crypto in the U.S. and divided industry oversight between the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). More regulation in the U.S., such as the Genius Act that was passed last year , has supported crypto prices. But the Clarity Act failing to pass could still boost prices, as the SEC and CFTC will set the rules for now, Hougan said. "It's the most pro-crypto SEC in the history of the U.S.; it's the most pro-crypto CFTC in the history of the U.S. So ironically, in the absence of Clarity passing, we may actually have stronger pro-crypto regulation," Hougan said. The Bitwise CIO also said that investors are rotating out of AI stocks back into crypto. He added that the AI boom had "sucked all the oxygen out of the room. Any investor who was a momentum-driven investor was focused on that. Now that that has sort of levelled off, you're seeing that money rotate back into crypto." - CNBC's Tanaya Macheel and Garrett Downs contributed to this report.

events.title: Saudi Arabia ramps up Gulf oil exports after pipeline attack, data shows
events.summary: Fuel tanks at the fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has increased loadings from Gulf export terminals after an attack earlier this month disrupted shipments. LONDON - Saudi Aramco loaded about 14 million barrels of crude oil on seven VLCCs inside the Mid-east Gulf on Sept 20, data from TankerTrackers.com showed, as the kingdom increased loadings from Gulf export terminals after an attack disrupted shipments via its east-west pipeline to the Red Sea. The loadings add to signs of a partial recovery in Saudi shipments, with expectations of higher volumes weighing on oil prices on Sept 21 and helping push the Brent benchmark below US$100 (S$127) a barrel for the first time since Sept 9. Satellite images seen by Reuters appear to show seven tankers near Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura port on Sept 20. An Aramco spokesperson declined to comment. The loading of seven tankers would suggest an increase in Saudi supplies. JP Morgan analysts said in a Sept 18 note that satellite data indicated Saudi oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 2.9 million barrels per day over the past six days, up from just 700,000 bpd in August. Drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its east-west oil pipeline on Sept 13, halting crude loadings at the kingdom’s Yanbu oil port on the Red Sea. As a result, Aramco cancelled some crude cargo sales to European clients , while boosting sales to Asia for crude it loads at its eastern ports inside the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia sold about 60 million barrels of crude from its Ras Tanura port inside the Strait of Hormuz for loading via ship-to-ship transfer at the Omani port of Sohar this month and next, trade sources told Reuters last week. events.title: Celebrity deaths in 2026: Remembering the famous people we lost this year
events.summary: Duncan Sheik. Bruce Glikas/Getty Images Actors James Van Der Beek, Hayden Panettiere, Robert Duvall, Chuck Norris, and Tim Curry died in 2026. So did musicians Dolly Parton and Duncan Sheik. Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, activist Gloria Steinem, and media mogul Ted Turner also died this year. Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Scott Adams, 68 Scott Adams. Michael Macor/Getty Images Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert." By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips. At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons. Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams. Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer . Brad Arnold, 47 Brad Arnold. Scott Gries/ImageDirect/Getty Images The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year. The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom. Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer. Afrika Bambaataa, 68 Afrika Bambaataa. Paul Natkin/WireImage/Getty A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx. He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career. Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse . Bambaataa denied all claims. He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer . Rob Bass, 59 Rob Bass. Al Pereira/Michael Osche Archives/Getty Images One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstram, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock. The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine. Bass died on May 22 following cancer . Nicholas Brendon, 54 Nicholas Brendon. Getty Images Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer." He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential." Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement. In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries. "While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart." Peabo Bryson, 75 Peabo Bryson. ABC Photo Archives/Getty Images Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads. Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain." Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin." Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given. James Burrows, 85 James Burrows. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier." Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes. Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given. Kyle Busch, 41 Kyle Busch. Sean Gardner/Getty Images Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time. Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead. Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis. Robert Carradine, 71 Robert Carradine. Bobby Bank/WireImage/Getty Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds." As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career. He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series. Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness. "We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness." Carradine died by suicide on February 23. If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline . Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US. Bud Cort, 77 Bud Cort. CBS Photo Archive/CBS via Getty Images Most famous for his role as Harold in the 1971 cult-classic "Harold and Maude," Bud Cort became the epitome of 1970s counterculture thanks to his baby-faced looks, wit, and sophisticated persona. events.title: What is the White House press pool and why does it matter?
events.summary: The White House press pool covers and travels with the U.S. president every day, providing the public with a near-constant stream of information on the leader's activities. Other media outlets can use the pool's work, ensuring news and footage of the president are widely disseminated to news organizations around the world. President Donald Trump's press ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico, and subsequent suspension of the TV pool, could limit the public's view into his White House. The White House press pool covers and travels with the U.S. president every day, providing news outlets and the public with a near-constant stream of information on the leader's activities. With the television pool suspending coverage of President Donald Trump after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, the public could be deprived of critical information about the president's activities. The five networks that have made up the White House television pool — ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and NBC News — rotate each day by having one network that covers the president's daily movements in Washington and around the world and remarks he makes. They feed video to other news organizations, and it airs on television stations while also being used by journalists who are not in those spaces to report in real time what the president says. The pool covers events that are widely open to the press and is in more limited spaces like awaiting the president underneath the wing of Air Force One and travelling with him aboard the plane. The pool also allows the press to be present — and therefore the public to have access to information — in spaces like the Oval Office, which does not have enough room to accommodate all of the hundreds of reporters covering the White House. The pool has chronicled U.S. presidents every day for nearly a century, since the presidency of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, according to the White House Correspondents' Association , which represents journalists who cover the White House and advocates for access to the president. Pool reporters brought the nation live coverage of events including the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Broadcast, still photographers, print or digital and radio reporters cover the president at the White House and when he travels, from each day's initial "call time" to when a "lid" is called — the time when staff alerts reporters that the White House says the president will not be seen again for the day. For most of the press pool's history, the White House Correspondents' Association controlled which outlets covered the president on any given day. In recent years, this typically included a TV crew — a slot that rotated between ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — a rotating "print" newspaper slot, a radio slot, and dedicated slots for still photographers and "wire" services like The Associated Press, Reuters and Bloomberg. Trump's White House, however, has taken a heavier hand in pool coverage. In February 2025, the White House press office announced it would take control of determining the press pool that covered Trump. The administration has since made several changes to the composition of the pool that covers Trump, including the additions of secondary TV and print reporters and the elimination of the "wire" slot. The White House also added a "new media" seat, for which outlets not typically included in the press pool can apply to be chosen for by the White House press office. Outlets in the new media seat have ranged from right-wing influencers to startup media outlets. According to a 2025 analysis from the Poynter Institute , the White House's selection of the secondary TV and new media slot reporters has skewed towards conservative outlets. The Trump administration also tried to suspend a CNN reporter's press credential in 2018 — although the attempt was unsuccessful and the reporter's credential was soon restored. In 2009, the Obama administration's Treasury Department attempted to exclude Fox News from a series of TV pool interviews with executive-pay czar Kenneth R. Feinberg amid tension between the Obama administration and the network. The administration, however, reversed course after pushback from the included TV outlets. Trump administration advances $24.3 billion F-35 deal to Saudi Arabia Bill to curb AI data center utility costs hits snag in Senate House heads home to campaign amid calls for urgent AI action The pool gives the public extensive access to the president's activity and lets the president quickly summon reporters when the White House wants to widely disseminate information. The pool, which is coordinated by the White House Correspondents' Association, includes rotating representatives from participating news outlets, which pay for their journalists' travel with the president. Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC Forbes published its 2026 list of the top 400 billionaires in the US on Tuesday. Many of the US' youngest billionaires owe their fortunes to artificial intelligence startups. Steven Hao, cofounder and CTO of Cognition, is the Forbes 400's youngest billionaire. New money is in for America's young and rich. Forbes released its annual list of America's 400 richest billionaires in September, and a record $4.4 billion net worth was required to make the cut. Just 10 of those billionaires are under 40, up from four on last year's list. And most of them didn't inherit their wealth. The majority of the US' youngest Forbes 400 billionaires — seven of them — got their money from the AI boom as founders. Of those seven, four come from one company: Anthropic , the AI company founded only five years ago and now valued at $1.5 trillion in the secondary market . Anthropic's seven cofounders all vowed earlier this year to donate 80% of their personal wealth to philanthropic causes. The other three are founders of Surge AI, OpenAI, and Cognition. Only one billionaire on the list — Lukas Walton — inherited their wealth from a family fortune. Walton is the grandson of Walmart founder Sam Walton and is also one of two young billionaires who do not live in California. The other, Edwin Chen, lives in New York. events.title: I left my job at 50 and retired to Mexico. After 3 years, there are 5 things I'd tell any American hoping to do the same.
events.summary: Retiring abroad early was challenging but worth it for me. Ivy Ge At 50, I left my full-time job as a pharmacist in the US and retired abroad in Mexico. I wish I'd tested living in my new city for a long period and learned more Spanish before I left. Those trying to retire abroad early should get their finances in order as soon as they can. In 2023, at 50 years old, I left my career as a pharmacist in California and moved to Ajijic, Mexico. Three years later, I'm waking up to bird calls and watching avocados grow in my backyard. It hasn't been an easy journey, but it's been a worthwhile one. Here are a few things I'd tell any American who's also hoping to retire abroad in their 50s . Start stress-testing countries (and neighborhoods) as soon as you can Vacationing in a place isn't the same as living there. Ivy Ge Before I moved, I treated Mexico like a vacation destination rather than a place I'd actually live in. And if a place looked nice in pictures or on a quick tour, I believed I'd found "the one." This thinking turned out to be a big mistake. For example, in late 2022, I was vacationing in Puerto Vallarta , a trip I'd planned long before I decided to retire in Mexico. But by the time I flew out, I'd bought my one-way ticket to Ajijic and was actively hunting for a place to live. Since I was already in Mexico, I figured I could just squeeze in a quick visit to Ajijic and line up rentals. One by one, my viewing appointments were canceled. The only house available during my short trip was much larger and more expensive than I'd budgeted. It was beautiful, and I loved it so much that I ended up signing a yearlong lease — something I'm confident I would've resisted if I'd taken the time to know the area first. Soon, I discovered the frequent, loud block parties in front of the house that lasted until early morning. Eventually, I broke the lease at a loss and moved to a quiet neighborhood away from all the action in the town center. In time, I realized I wanted to live in a quieter area. Ivy Ge Looking back, I needed months in Ajijic, not days, to explore different neighborhoods and find the one that fit my needs. No matter where you go, a short resort stay won't show you what it's like to live somewhere full time. Seasons and tourist cycles change traffic, noise, and prices. After researching your dream retirement country , plan an extended stay during a less favorable season and rent in local neighborhoods rather than popular tourist areas. Build a financial cushion that's more than what you think you need I made sure my finances were mostly in order before I left the US. Ivy Ge To cover my living expenses and prepare for emergencies, I set up  high‑yield savings accounts , CDs, bonds, and money‑market funds while working with a financial advisor to grow my long‑term investments before I left. However, in the first months of my early retirement , the lack of a paycheck felt jarring. I was anxious watching money go out but not come in. On top of that, the US-dollar-to-Mexican peso exchange rate dropped sharply in 2023, so my money didn't go as far as I expected. Inflation and surprise expenses, such as large repair costs and frequent flights home for family emergencies, also added to my financial concerns. As I settled in, I learned to reduce expenses by finding better-priced stores and services. I set up a dollar‑to‑peso exchange-rate alert and converted money in batches when rates were favorable, so I felt less at the mercy of rate fluctuations . Working with a financial advisor also keeps me grounded. I know exactly how much I can spend each year until my pension and Social Security kick in, and I put what's left toward travel in Mexico and beyond. Have the hard conversations with your loved ones early on It wasn't easy to move away from my mom, but I knew it was the best choice for me. Ivy Ge I sat down with my mom before I moved to Mexico . She wanted to stay near her friends in San Francisco; I needed a lower‑cost, comfortable environment to pursue creative work. She worried I wouldn't be around to help out. I promised weekly calls and twice‑yearly visits, and I kept managing her medical appointments and medications from afar. Before I left, I helped her move into an independent senior-living apartment building with a staffed front desk and around-the-clock on-call support. We message each other almost daily, sharing things we find online. We talk more now than we did when I lived 20 minutes away, and our bond has grown stronger because of the distance. If you're thinking of retiring abroad, bring your family into the conversation early so they have time to understand your plans and stay connected. Don't wait to build the life skills you'll need — or to prepare for the identity shift that comes with retirement Retiring was a huge identity shift for me, since I'd spent so long working toward and building a career that I was now giving up. Ivy Ge Moving abroad often means learning a new language. I wish I'd started learning Spanish long before my move. Since Ajijic is a popular town for American expats , I can get by on basic phrases. Once I venture out, though, Spanish becomes essential. So I began taking lessons on Baselang, an online tutoring platform with native Latin American instructors. I'm still far from fluent, but I've talked soccer with my gardener, been invited to weddings, and gained a deeper understanding of Mexican culture. Language is one thing, but identity is another. With early retirement, my identity as a health professional disappeared overnight. I had moved with a clear intention to write, but it was still a shock to lose the role I'd held for years. I used to counsel patients on weaning off potent medications to ease withdrawal symptoms. Now I suggest "weaning off" your old profession by reducing your reliance on work for your identity while building your new one through classes, communities, or side projects. Start with one thing that energizes you or a skill you've always wanted to learn, and build your daily structure around it before you retire, not after. Retirement is a big change, and so is living in a new country. When you combine both things, uncertainty is inevitable, but patience and resourcefulness go a long way. Treat the first year as an experiment Ultimately, my first year in Mexico was worth all of the challenges. Ivy Ge Even with meticulous planning, things will go differently than you expect. Instead of trying to make everything right, focus on the big pieces — housing, healthcare, legal status — and accept that smaller decisions might not work out perfectly. I made plenty of mistakes during my first year in Mexico , but each one made me wiser. What helped was treating them as learning curves and character-building opportunities rather than permanent realities. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Rent-a-GPU firm reportedly seeks a valuation of up to $35B in New York IPO Meta Muse AI app flaw lets local malware redirect dictation traffic now AWS bolts together open source agent harness, says it sips fewer tokens than rivals 4 hours ago Schneider says hotter coolant can make AI datacenters less thirsty 5 hours ago Amazon shows Meta's Muse AI shopping agent the door 6 hours ago Google joins the ‘Oops, our agents hacked someone’ club after partner’s internet access error 16 hours ago London-based neocloud Nscale has filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange after expanding rapidly on the back of the AI infrastructure boom. The rent-a-GPU business, which emerged from cryptocurrency miner Arkon Energy, filed a Form S-1 registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Friday. It intends to list under the ticker NSCL. The document does not specify the number of shares it'll offer, their expected price, or the valuation Nscale hopes to achieve.The Financial Times previously reported that the company was targeting a valuation of up to $35 billion. The filing shows how costly Nscale's expansion has been. Revenue surged from $10.4 million to $140.6 million in the six months to June 30, but its net loss widened from $368.9 million to $1.02 billion over the same period. Nscale reported $103.4 billion in active and contracted total contract value (TCV) as of August 31, up from $38 billion at the end of 2025. That figure is not recognized revenue or a conventional backlog: only $2.6 billion was attached to active contracts, and delivery of the remainder depends on projects being financed and built. Agreements with Anthropic account for up to circa $44.6 billion, although Nscale warned it had not secured binding commitments for the financing required to fulfill them. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are acting as lead bookrunners for the offering. Nscale, which operates datacenters in Europe and the US, describes itself as a full-stack AI cloud provider, offering infrastructure and software for training and running AI models. Its projects include an AI campus announced last year for OpenAI in Norway and the Monarch Compute Campus in West Virginia, developed with Nvidia and Microsoft. Its board includes former British deputy prime minister Sir Nick Clegg , former Meta chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, and former Yahoo president Susan Decker. As The Register recently reported , Tracxn data shows that Nscale has attracted nearly two-thirds of the equity funding raised by UK datacenter infrastructure companies. It was also the sector's only privately held company valued at more than $1 billion. Despite its London headquarters and prominence in Britain's AI infrastructure sector, Nscale chose New York rather than London for its proposed listing. The company did not answer our question about why it selected the US exchange. The calculation echoes Arm's decision to list in New York : Wall Street offers a deeper pool of technology-focused capital and the prospect of higher valuations than London.

events.title: Stock boom is fueling a ‘retirement party,’ economists say — what it means for workers
events.summary: Stocks have posted double-digit annual returns since 2023, largely on the back of euphoria over artificial intelligence. The stock surge has led to a "wealth effect" that has helped accelerate retirements among older workers, economists said. Their participation in the labor force has been "collapsing" since the summer of 2024, Bank of America economists wrote. A downturn in stocks poses financial risks for these new retirees, and would threaten the broader job market and economy. The stock market boom seems to be fueling a wave of retirements . Workers age 55 and older are leaving the labor force at a rapid pace, government data shows, a trend that coincides with ballooning stock wealth fueled by euphoria over artificial intelligence . The retirement surge among these workers is attributable in part to a "wealth effect," economists said: Workers near traditional retirement age have seen their stock portfolios swell and feel rich enough to finally leave their 9-to-5. In a research note last month, Bank of America economists referred to the trend as a "stock-fueled retirement party." "Labor force participation is collapsing among older workers," wrote the economists, Stephen Juneau and Aditya Bhave. "We think the strength of the equity market is partly to blame." Workforce exits among older workers have helped keep unemployment relatively low in recent years, economists said. Their departures help make space for job seekers and new entrants to the labor market, an important factor in an otherwise frozen job market , they said. However, if AI optimism wanes and the stock market sours, it could mean bad news for these recent retirees, the U.S. labor market and the economy, economists said. The labor force includes people who have a job and unemployed people who are looking for work. The labor force participation rate is the percentage of people who are in the labor force. Participation among workers 55 years and older initially declined sharply in the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic, as it did for the broader pool of workers, too. However, labor force participation among older workers "never recovered" after the pandemic, Bank of America economists wrote. It stayed "range-bound" until the summer of 2024, but "has taken another big leg down since then," they wrote. Since August 2024, the labor force participation rate for workers age 55 and older has declined from 38.6% to 37.2%, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data . Taxing high earners to help fund Social Security gains bipartisan attention Trump announces $500 Obamacare refunds for nearly 1 million people As Republicans tout Trump's 'big beautiful bill,' here's who the tax breaks benefited IRS tax debt agreements have plummeted: 'I've never seen a number that low' CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Meanwhile, the S&P 500 stock index yielded a string of double-digit returns for investors in recent years: 26% in 2023, 25% in 2024 and 18% in 2025, including reinvested dividends, according to data compiled by Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at New York University. The index is up about 16% so far in 2026, as of early Monday. The resulting wealth surge, including in people's retirement accounts like 401(k) plans, likely made the choice to retire an easier one for many people, said Thomas Ryan, a North America economist at Capital Economics. The net worth of households and nonprofits increased by $12.8 trillion, to $195.9 trillion, in the second quarter of 2026, driven primarily by strong stock returns, according to Federal Reserve data . That's by far the largest quarterly wealth increase on record since 2000, when the central bank started tracking the statistic, according to a CNBC analysis of Fed data. "It puts people in a position where they can retire early, because they're in a favorable [financial] position," Ryan said. Of course, near-retirees may be unlikely to be fully invested in stocks. Financial advisors generally recommend shifting to a more conservative asset allocation leading up to and in retirement, to avoid subjecting one's whole nest egg to the volatility of the stock market. However, the typical 65-year-old might still have a relatively large allocation to stocks — perhaps 50%, for example, with the remainder in assets like bonds and cash . Stocks are the traditional growth engine of an investment portfolio, and provide a hedge against the rising cost of living over a retirement that may last many decades. "If people weren't feeling confident enough that they could afford to retire, they wouldn't — and we'd see a very different story in the data," said Michael Reid, head of U.S. economics at the Royal Bank of Canada. Wealth effect compounds demographics That said, the wealth effect isn't the only factor pushing down labor force participation among older workers.

events.title: Michael Saylor’s Strategy buys Bitcoin again as surprise rally pushes price above $85,000
events.summary: Bitcoin has been rising during a month that has historically been bearish for the asset. Strategy, the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin holder, bought 950 Bitcoin for nearly $76 million over the past week, according to its latest financial disclosure. The purchase marked the company’s first Bitcoin acquisition in roughly three weeks and lifted Strategy’s total holdings to 846,000 Bitcoin. It coincided with the price of Bitcoin surging more than 6% over the past 24 hours to nearly $86,000, and led to a jump in Strategy shares of nearly 9% to $167. The rise in Strategy’s share price was also helped by the company spending $174 million to repurchase STRC, its dividend-paying preferred shares. Strategy, led by the flamboyant billionaire Michael Saylor, is an outsize player in the Bitcoin market as it holds around 4% of the total supply. The latest rise in Bitcoin’s price has extended the cryptocurrency’s recovery from a yearlong bear market. Bitcoin fell as low as $58,000 in June, roughly 53% below its $125,000 price last October.  The volatility has directly affected Strategy, whose vast Bitcoin holdings have made its stock a proxy for the cryptocurrency. Saylor has long championed a “never sell your Bitcoin” mantra, but in the past four months his company has sold Bitcoin four times.  As Bitcoin’s decline squeezed the company’s finances, Strategy created STRC last year to raise cash from investors for more Bitcoin purchases. The preferred shares pay investors regular dividends. As the cryptocurrency rebounded over the past month, Strategy returned to buying, making two purchases. Its latest STRC buyback also reduced the company’s future payments to investors. Strategy’s fortunes remain closely tied to Bitcoin’s price, but its return to buying suggests the company sees enough support for the cryptocurrency’s recovery to resume accumulating it, Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at the financial technology firm IG Group, told Fortune . “When you want to buy into a rising market, what August and September have given you is the potential for that to continue in a more sustained fashion. That’s just what Saylor and the rest of the team really want to see,” he said.  Strategy’s latest purchase was modest compared with some of its earlier acquisitions. Beauchamp said the smaller buy does not necessarily point to a particular concern, but may reflect a strategy of adding Bitcoin gradually as its price climbs. The Bessent effect Bitcoin’s renewed buying pressure came in mid-August after the U.S. Treasury announced that it would double purchases of older long-term government bonds. The cryptocurrency had spent months in a downturn as investors focused on faster-moving themes such as artificial intelligence, but worries about government bonds, rising yields, and inflation revived Bitcoin’s appeal as an alternative asset, Beauchamp explained. “You always need a narrative to kickstart something,” he said. “With Bessent’s moves back to treasuries, suddenly it seemed like this was sort of the dream scenario for Bitcoin.” The rally gathered pace as markets digested the Federal Reserve’s latest interest-rate hike. Crypto markets have often struggled when the Fed raises rates because higher borrowing costs can reduce the money investors devote to riskier assets. When Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced a quarter-point rate increase on Sept. 16, Bitcoin initially fell to about $75,600, erasing gains it had made earlier that month. But the decline proved short-lived, and Bitcoin soon resumed its ascent. Once the widely expected rate hike took place, “a more rational approach to the future applies,” with a key source of uncertainty out of the way, Beauchamp said. events.title: The summit won’t break the US-China stalemate
events.summary: Andy’s view In Mao Zedong’s 1938 essay , penned during the Japanese invasion of China, he divided conflict into three phases: strategic defense, strategic stalemate, and strategic counter-offensive. On the eve of a leaders’ summit this week in Washington, US-China ties are stuck in the stalemate stage, deadlocked on everything from trade and technology to Taiwan — and it’s only a matter of time before hostilities ramp back up. Of course, there’s the mercurial Trump factor, which throws off any tidy analysis. The US president plans to personally greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Andrews Air Base this week — an honor normally reserved for popes and close partners — and has been conciliatory to Beijing ahead of these talks. But Trump could just as easily flip, perhaps if Republicans are routed in November’s midterms, as he did at the end of his first term when he blamed China and COVID-19 — “kung-flu” — for his election defeat. And stalemate isn’t quite the same thing as a truce. Beneath the diplomatic surface, the two sides are radically at odds over just about everything: Beijing’s role in providing a financial (and, reportedly, tactical) lifeline for Iran as it lashes out at its Gulf neighbors and the US; keeping Russia’s economy afloat as it pummels Ukraine; tariffs, sanctions, currency levels, student visas, and much more. Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary running point on the summit, once likened the superpowers’ relationship to a game of water polo : Above the water, the two teams toss the ball back and forward; below, legs kick and flail. But in a stalemate, the most awkward problems either get ignored or deferred. Trump’s extravagant welcome gesture will almost certainly be matched by prosaic summit outcomes. A Financial Times headline summed up the low expectations : “The main Trump-Xi summit achievement will be it happening at all.” A case in point is the activation of the Board of Trade, an arrangement agreed upon at the leaders’ meeting in Busan, South Korea, that is explicitly designed to avoid the tough issues. China is demanding the US ease export bans on high-tech goods, like chipmaking gear; the US bitterly complains about Chinese overproduction and transhipment. The trade board, however, limits itself to “non-sensitive” consumer products — flip flops, toys, and kitchenware. On AI safety — arguably the most significant topic on the agenda, given the risks of an AI-induced blow-up ( CNN reports a recent close call involving a Chinese ship in the Middle East, wrongly identified by a US chatbot to be carrying nuclear material) — it isn’t even clear the two sides are talking about the same thing. In the US, AI safety refers to existential risk; in China, it means preserving regime stability. As always, Xi’s priority is saving the party that he leads — that’s why he was selected for the job — and a good summit outcome would be simply prolonging the superpower standoff, at least until a party gathering next year that’s expected to hand him a fourth five-year term in office. To borrow Mao’s parlance, Xi’s not ready yet for the strategic counter-offensive stage. Among the proposals put forward by the Trump administration is a regular AI dialogue , alongside setting up something akin to an AI crisis hotline. The offer is perhaps unintentionally symbolic of the countries’ stasis — limited in scope and ambition even as they grapple with huge geopolitical and societal instability. It’s even unclear whether an AI hotline mechanism would work. Decades ago, their militaries installed a telephone link to be used in the event of an emergency. One arrived in 2001 when a US spy plane limped into Hainan Island with a 24-member crew after a collision with a Chinese fighter jet that killed its pilot. The American side made a frantic call: Nobody picked up. Notable China holds “escalation dominance” over the US when it comes to economic conflict , but that “would not spare its own economy pain if it were forced into a tit-for-tat conflict with Washington ,” Adam Posen argued in Foreign Affairs.

Driving the news: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend discussed a U.S.-China AI dialogue to notify the other country when AI incidents reached national security risk levels. The devil is in the details and OpenAI is proposing solutions that CEO Sam Altman will cover in his address at the United Nations Security Council in New York on Wednesday. What they're saying: OpenAI recommends leveraging AI safety institutes around the world to facilitate standard-setting through the U.S. Center for AI Security and Innovation, which is part of the Commerce Department. The company also recommends shared global measurements for classifying incidents and how to track, report and respond to alignment issues. The goal is to have international standards for incidents that happen before deployment in test settings and those that occur in the real world, an OpenAI official told Axios. What we're watching: Expect AI labs to continue chiming in as all eyes are on President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's meetings and a state dinner featuring industry heavy hitters later this week.

events.title: China expels two top ‘disloyal’ military leaders from Communist Party
events.summary: China removes two top generals over corruption, disloyalty as part of an ongoing anti-corruption crackdown. China has expelled two top military generals from the Chinese Communist Party on suspicion of corruption and other serious misconduct, becoming the latest senior officials to fall afoul of a significant anti-corruption push by President Xi Jinping. Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli “seriously violated political discipline and political rules, formed cliques and factions, and were disloyal and dishonest to the party”, state-run Xinhua news agency reported on Monday, citing official documents. No details of the alleged crimes were provided. list 1 of 4 US tariffs against Russian oil buyers pass: What it means for China, India list 2 of 4 Can the US win the AI cold war with China? list 3 of 4 Why have China’s oil prices reached a record high? list 4 of 4 Can AI regulation keep America ahead of China? Investigations into the pair were announced in January, and they were removed from the military in late August. Zhang was long seen as Xi’s closest military ally as second-in-command of the Central Military Commission, China’s supreme command body. Liu was a CMC member and the chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department. The expulsions are part of the president’s sweeping anti-corruption crackdown, with thousands of officials being purged and millions within the Chinese bureaucracy investigated. The campaign is among the largest in modern Chinese history, including prior removals of high-profile political rivals. In June 2024 , Defence Minister Li Shangfu and his predecessor were expelled from the party as part of the crackdown. More than a year later, China dismissed the second-highest-ranking general and eight other senior officials from the military and party. The military has become an increasing target of the anti-corruption purges, leaving two active members – including Xi serving as chairman – on the formerly seven-member CMC. The Defence Ministry announcement was made days before the Chinese president is set to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington, and weeks before a key Communist Party assembly on internal governance.

events.title: Nissan eyes increasing U.S. production as new Rogue hybrid launches
events.summary: Nissan Motor is considering increasing its U.S. production with the launch of its 2027 Rogue crossover, Christian Meunier, chairman of Nissan Americas, told CNBC. The Japanese automaker currently has two production shifts at its assembly plant in Smyrna, Tennessee, and adding another could mean hundreds, if not thousands, of new jobs. Nissan is also rolling out a new hybrid model with the Rogue that it views as a crucial offering for American consumers. Nissan Motor is looking to increase its U.S. production as it launches the 2027 Rogue crossover, including with a new hybrid model that the company views as a crucial offering for American consumers. "We're now maxing out the production capacity in the U.S.," Christian Meunier, chairman of Nissan Americas, told CNBC. "The next step is going to be three shifts, and I'm pretty optimistic that with the launch of the new Rogue that is happening in the next couple months, we'll be able to do that pretty quickly with the launch of the hybrid." The Japanese automaker currently produces the Rogue alongside other Nissan and Infiniti crossovers at a 6 million-square-foot assembly plant on two production shifts in Smyrna, Tennessee . It also has another large manufacturing plant producing the Nissan Altima sedan and Frontier midsize pickup truck in Canton, Mississippi. Additional production at assembly plants typically means hundreds, if not thousands, of new jobs. Nissan's moves come as the Trump administration has been focused on increasing employment and domestic production in the U.S. auto industry. U.S. manufacturing of the hybrid is expected to start next year after the spring production launch of the 2027 Rogue with a traditional gas engine at the Tennessee plant. In the meantime, Meunier said Nissan plans to import the hybrid vehicles from Japan as a way to get them to market more quickly to lift sales and help with an ongoing global turnaround plan for the company. Meunier said if Nissan can add a third shift to each of its assembly plants, it would boost the automaker's U.S. production to roughly 1 million units annually, up from nearly 487,000 in 2025. Nissan has a target to produce 80% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. domestically by 2030, but the company has no plans for a new plant as of now. "I think we're very well equipped to succeed without major investment and a new factory and everything else. Maybe after 2030," he said. "Over the next four or five years, we'll see." Nissan on Monday officially revealed the 2027 Rogue with its new "e-Power" technology for the U.S., which is the first hybrid of its kind for the American market. The "e-Power" system is called a series hybrid. It uses the engine as a generator to power the vehicle's electric motors that then propel the vehicle. It operates like emerging extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, but has a smaller battery and doesn't require a plug. It also does not use the engine to power the wheels, just electric motors. Meunier said the Rogue hybrid and resurrecting the Xterra off-road SUV were his top vehicle priorities when he rejoined Nissan in January 2025 after four and a half years with Jeep. That included pulling ahead the Rogue hybrid twice for the U.S. Nissan said Monday that the starting pricing of the Rogue hybrid will be between $35,490 for the entry-level model to $43,490 for a "Platinum" version. The Rogue is a sales leader for the company in the U.S. It competes in the highly competitive small crossover segment against the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V, which have the best-selling hybrid options in that category. "The hybrid power that we're launching on Rogue is going to really be the boost to our performance," Meunier said. "It's been quite remarkable to be able to grow without having a hybrid in the U.S. because the hybrids are obviously becoming more and more popular." Meunier said Nissan plans to position the Rogue e-Power squarely against the Toyota RAV4. He said that may include an unconventional sales option to allow potential customers to test drive both vehicles at Nissan dealerships, which wouldn't typically have a Toyota available. The focus on the Rogue hybrid comes after Nissan and other automakers lost billions of dollars on all-electric vehicles amid a pullback in regulatory support as well as lackluster consumer demand. Nissan has said the e-Power is a better solution than EVs or even traditional hybrids for U.S. consumers, especially amid inflated fuel prices due to the Iran war. "It's going to make people look at Nissan with different eyes," Meunier said. "A lot of customers that didn't even consider us until the hybrid comes to market." Nissan said the fuel economy for the Rogue hybrid will be 38 miles per gallon combined. That compares to the Toyota RAV4 hybrid at 43 miles mpg and the Honda CR-V at 40 mpg. Nissan's renewed focus on the U.S. comes amid a global turnaround plan.
