events.title: Shein, Temu shoppers do not feel responsible for environmental concerns, study finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ultra-fast fashion buyers feel a lack of personal responsibility despite environmental concerns A new study of ultra-fast fashion buyers found price was one of the biggest shopping motivators. ( AP: Richard Drew ) Shoppers of ultra-fast fashion companies, such as Shein and Temu, say despite being aware of environmental and ethical concerns, other factors such as price, convenience and not feeling personally responsible keep them coming back. A new study published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing this week found millennials, who frequently expressed concern about ethical and sustainability issues, often did not translate this concern into purchasing behaviour. The study surveyed 20 Australian millennials who shopped on ultra-fast fashion sites about what informed their purchasing behaviours. It found affordability, convenience, promotions, social media trends, novelty, variety and social validation were the biggest purchase drivers. For some, affordability meant they were likely to purchase styles they may not usually try and make riskier choices. You can get five things for the price of one at other places. I can redo my wardrobe every season without hurting my bank account. It's perfect when I need something quick and cheap for an event. The study also found the purchases were usually not spontaneous, with many shoppers saying they saved carts and waited for a sale before purchasing. When I see a 70 per cent off notification, it's almost impossible not to look. It feels like I'm losing money if I don't buy it. Sales get me every time. I've bought outfits I didn't even wear just because they were on sale. I add things to my cart and wait for payday or a discount notification. Study co-author Carol Tan, who is an associate professor at the School of Fashion and Textiles at RMIT University, said this behaviour was known as "strategic spontaneity". "You think it's impulsive, but it's actually planned," she said. "So what people do is they save the items, they have a wish list, and then they monitor their sales and wait for payday. "It could be sitting in their cart for a week or a month, and then a spur-of-the-moment decision is when they actually make the purchase and it happens in minutes." Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au The fast and ultra-fast fashion gap While fast fashion has been around for some time, platforms such as Shein and Temu differ in their production and distribution methods. Traditional fast-fashion brands release a new collection every two to four weeks that can range from hundreds to thousands of styles and sell primarily through physical stores. Ultra-fast fashion stores produce 2,000 to 10,000 new styles daily and use digital-only, mobile app-dominant sales models. Dr Tan said the rise of ultra-fast fashion has pushed some fast-fashion brands to change their strategy. "They are trying to not compete with the Sheins of the world and they are trying to go a bit more upmarket. So they sell better-quality stuff and they have like $400 jackets," she said. Outside of the growing price gap between fast fashion and ultra-fashion fashion, Dr Tan said these sites often sold items you could not buy in brick-and-mortar stores. Despite participants expressing concerns about the environmental and ethical impacts of ultra-fast fashion brands, many still continued to purchase on Shein or Temu. According to the latest figures from the Australia Institute, on average Australians purchase 56 items of clothing a year. It also reports more than 200,000 tonnes of clothing end up in Australian landfills each year. The study found participants were more influenced by social and economic drivers than long-term ethical concerns. I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out. I try to buy sustainable brands, but they are so expensive. Shein is just there and it's easy. If the big brands are allowed to sell it, then it can't be all my fault for buying it. I feel bad sometimes, but one small top isn't going to destroy the ocean. The study also found buyers would draw on explanations such as reduced feelings of personal responsibility, affordability constraints, limited access to sustainable alternatives and the belief that the individual purchases had little impact. In some countries, different taxes have been introduced to deter buyers from ultra-fast fashion brands. France has banned advertising from ultra-fast fashion businesses and introduced a fee that will rise to €10 ($16) per item by 2030. New Zealand has a levy of NZ$2.21 ($1.80) per package.

events.title: Charity provides school lunches for kids as food insecurity rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts National school lunch program launched in Moe aims to tackle food insecurity Victoria and Brandon are big fans of the Spoonfull program. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) A new universal school meals program launched in Moe offers healthy lunches to primary school children. The program aims to tackle food insecurity as well as improving student wellbeing and learning outcomes. The charity Eat Up hopes to roll out the program across Australia to schools in need. It is lunchtime at Elizabeth Street Primary School at Moe in Victoria's east. On today's menu, a chicken pasta bake is the hot option, and tuna and salad rolls are on offer for others. The children queuing up are told that the more they can stack on their plates, the better. "I love the food, it's amazing," student Victoria says. "My favourite has been the lasagne and butter chicken, and I really like the wraps they make. "They give options to us that if we don't like a food, then we can just try it and I just love how they do that." A team of volunteers helps to prepare the students' lunches. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The lunches are part of a program that aims to tackle child hunger and improve student wellbeing across the country. The charity Eat Up has launched its pilot program Spoonfull at the school, a universal meal program that provides every student at participating schools with a healthy lunch, every day. Ian Frost and Carol O'Reilly say they have seen a huge improvement since the program was introduced. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The program was officially launched at Elizabeth Street Primary School in its purpose-built Hearts and Hands Learning Kitchen, after some strong lobbying by the school's wellbeing officer Carol O'Reilly. "I could see a need. I've been at this school for 17 years and I noticed running [the school's] breakfast club that kids are coming in without sandwiches," Ms O'Reilly said. "Now I know they're going out for recess with a full belly." She said learning outcomes and student welfare had improved greatly since the introduction of the program. "The kids are smiling. You can see them outside, they're playing and they're just dying to know what's for lunch." Students are offered a variety of healthy foods, including a hot lunch. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) School principal Ian Frost said the school lunch program had a positive impact on what students eat and had led to improved wellbeing and academic performance. Eat Up has been running for 15 years, delivering more than 6 million free on-demand school lunches to children experiencing food insecurity. Charity founder Lyndon Galea said the Spoonfull program built upon that business model to offer something more sustainable for schools to support students long-term. "This is different to our core model, [where] we have on-demand lunches, in terms of the cheese sandwiches, yoghurts and recess snacks," Mr Galea said. "We've learnt of certain schools where there's perhaps a higher number of kids arriving without food from home or where the socio-economic need bites even harder," he said. Lyndon Galea founded Eat Up 15 years ago. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) At Elizabeth Street Primary School, Spoonfull helped fund upgrades to the school kitchen to have commercial fridges and ovens, with hopes of also installing a dishwasher. Young people pushing back against artificial intelligence Rare century-old Mildura housing scheme directs lease revenue to local schools Loophole closed after rare private prosecution shuts Hepburn council Wilsons Prom's Sealers Cove track reopens after five years According to Australian Bureau of Statistics data from 2023, about 16 to 22 per cent of Australian children experience food insecurity. Single-parent households and low-income families were at the highest risk. As the cost of living continues to affect families, so too has the growth in food insecurity. "Families who are already in a difficult spot are needing help more often and then a lot of families who have historically been just above that level of need and needing support are accessing food support for the very first time," Mr Galea said. Through support from Spoonfull, the school was able to make key upgrades to its kitchen. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) Eat Up hopes to have enough support to roll out similar pilots in two additional schools. "I think it would be phenomenal for Australia and something our country can really take a big step forward [in]," Mr Galea said. Elizabeth Street Primary School student Victoria agreed and said she thought all schools could benefit from the program.

events.title: Trump to meet with Zelensky as Russia-Ukraine attacks intensify
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after a phone call with President Trump on Sunday that the two will meet this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Why it matters: The meeting comes as the White House works to broker an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to take reciprocal steps to deescalate and resume negotiations — and as fighting between the two sides has intensified in recent days. Zelensky's chief negotiator and the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, Rustem Umerov, told Axios he's been working with White House envoys in recent days to organize the meeting, which is expected to happen Tuesday. Driving the news: The meeting will take place several days after Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill and approved the biggest arms deal between the U.S. and Ukraine since assuming office — two steps Ukraine has been pushing for months. What he's saying: "An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelensky wrote on X. Zelensky said Ukraine is ready "to take really serious steps" to reach a deescalation deal with Russia. Behind the scenes: A source familiar with the call said Trump repeatedly asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The strikes are driving up global diesel prices. "The word diesel came up many times during the call," the source said. The intrigue: Earlier this week the Kyiv Independent reported that the Ukrainian government was "growing increasingly frustrated" with White House envoy Steve Witkoff. The story came out several days after Witkoff and Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time since the war began. Umerov told Axios the story was false. "I believe that the work of American negotiators should be assessed by people who are directly involved in the negotiation process and work closely with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," he said. He added that he's been working with Witkoff and Kushner on a daily basis over the last year. "Our main focus is on finding solutions for ending the war and gaining security guarantees and prosperity to Ukrainian people," he added. Umerov said the negotiations are under close public and media scrutiny and therefore "it comes with criticism." "Nevertheless, we need to stay focused. Steve has done a great job with us. We do not waste time and stay focused on finding solutions," he said. State of play: Umerov said significant progress has been made in the talks. "In particular, the number of stumbling blocks reduced from dozens to essentially one or two key issues that remain subject to negotiations," he said. "The trend is positive. The U.S. is super focused on the issue of stopping the war in Ukraine. The U.S. understands the situation on the battlefield, and signals to everyone that this terrible war should end," Umerov said. Yes, but: Hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have escalated in recent days, with both sides conducting more long-range attacks. On Sunday, Ukraine launched a missile attack on Moscow and hit an oil refinery. Russia has been launching missiles at Kyiv and other major cities almost every day in recent weeks. While Russia has signaled willingness to consider steps to deescalate ahead of winter — and a resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine — there has been little progress towards an actual deal.

events.title: Australians love these cars. Experts have 'real security concerns'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts We got a cybersecurity expert to hack this BYD. It was too easy On a narrow country road outside Canberra, I'm driving a BYD Shark 6, the hybrid ute loved by tradies and even a cabinet minister. But while I'm at the wheel, I'm not the only one in control; a hacker has access to the car. As the 2.6 tonne ute rounds a bend, he gets to work. With the stroke of a key, he kills the headlights, plunging me into darkness. The attack is not a total surprise. The Shark has spent the past two weeks with Dan Hreszczuk, a cybersecurity expert who specialises in cars. His task was to hack the vehicle and find out what could be seen and done remotely by the Shark's Chinese manufacturer. "It was easier than we were expecting," Hreszczuk says. Modern connected cars, particularly EVs and hybrids, are increasingly run by software, giving manufacturers the power to change, update and control vehicles, like never before. In the case of BYD and others, that software is controlled from China. With fuel prices on the rise, EVs and plug-in hybrids like the Shark have gone mainstream this year, making up almost a third of new cars sales to date. More than half of these are from Chinese brands. EVs, with all their sensors, cameras and microphones, hoover up and spit out vast amounts of data. Experts say that data poses a greater risk in the hands of Chinese EV makers because they can be compelled by the country's national security laws to co-operate with authorities. To put this potential access to the test, it made sense to pick a model from China's top EV brand, BYD. Hreszczuk, the co-founder of Fortify Labs in Canberra, was stunned by the BYD Shark's lack of cybersecurity. "The access we took advantage of didn't even have a password," he says. This lack of a password allowed Hreszczuk to access the car's digital arteries. From there it was a matter of unpicking the software programs which controlled different functions in the car. After two weeks, Hreszczuk was ready. Sitting by the side of the country road, he demonstrates what can be done with remote access to a vehicle. First, he locks the doors while I'm inside, blasts music over the speakers and plays images on the BYD's giant infotainment screen. Then, as I drive, he remotely switches the wipers on at top speed, sprays the windscreen with water and turns the lights on and off. The combination is unsettling and highly distracting. Adding to the distraction, Hreszczuk has the speaker telling me repeatedly: "For safety, use low beam." Fortunately, I was only travelling 30 kilometres per hour and the road was pretty straight. Then, Hreszczuk kills the lights altogether. Hreszczuk says he wasn't able to access more critical functions like brakes and cameras as these were well protected. But it doesn't take much imagination to understand how dangerous, even this kind of access could be in the hands of a malicious actor, with a vehicle travelling at high speed on a winding road. While sabotage is one worry, the concern most often cited is surveillance due to the array of cameras and microphones on an EV. Last year, the UK military banned Chinese EVs, even those made with Chinese components, from parking within 3 kilometres of some of its most sensitive locations. China itself has previously banned foreign EVs from military sites and political enclaves, aware of their surveillance potential. In Australia, there's no blanket ban on Chinese marques by Defence, but ASIO has warned ministers and public servants not to have sensitive conversations in their cars or connect work devices. But there's nothing to stop them owning a Chinese EV. Trade Minister Don Farrell has a BYD Shark 6, the same vehicle that Hreszczuk hacked. Farrell recently told a newspaper it's the "best ute I've ever owned". ASIO's surveillance fears appear well founded, based on what else Hreszczuk is able to do to with the Shark even at a low level of access. We devise a demonstration: I'll take the BYD for a drive around Canberra, and give my mother a call to talk her through some internet banking. As I drive past the war memorial and down Anzac Parade, Hreszczuk has already remotely accessed the vehicle and is tracking my progress. "How about we turn on the microphone?" he suggests to the crew back at his lab. At that point Hreszczuk can hear everything. When she picks up, I'm straight into the details of how I had set up her internet banking. "I'm going to use as a temporary password, my initials, the number of my house, and then my full date of birth. And then you can go in later and change it if you want," I tell her.

events.title: Is the AI industry really ready to slow down?
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt We’re seeing a big debate over AI safety and a potential slowdown, as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published a plan to “pace the frontier,” while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has publicly echoed President Donald Trump’s claims that the AI backlash is a hoax and regulation is unnecessary. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed whether executives like Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are serious about wanting to slow down. While I was surprised at how many industry leaders seemed to throw their support behind Amodei’s plan, Sean noted that the plan seemed short on details. And when Kristen asked whether a combination of existing regulation and the workings of the free market could provide enough safeguards on their own, Sean replied, “We have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here.” Plus, he argued, “There does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony: Sean, what do you think? Are we actually going to ”pace the frontier”? Sean: That sounds, for some reason, like something from “Point Break.” It’s just a very California statement, like, “We’re gonna pace the frontier, bruh.” I don’t know. I said on this show last week , I didn’t think we were headed for a slowdown of any kind, in large part because I don’t think these companies are structured in a way where that works. So this was a pretty immediate flip of what I said a week ago, to hear this from Dario at Anthropic and Sam at OpenAI and even Elon Musk to a certain degree — and we can get into whether we believe that or not. I will say, I don’t think I was completely wrong, because even with these loose plans that Dario laid out in a blog post and some of the other leaders have talked about, I feel like we’re still missing a lot of specifics here, not only on some of the claims about why these people think there are dangers and risks, but also specifics on what they mean by slowing down. Anthony, I know you read this stuff pretty closely last weekend as it was all popping off, so I’m curious if you’re maybe more generous than I am, as far as understanding what it is they’re trying to say here. Anthony: I mean, I also have questions. What really stood out to me is the fact that so many people in the industry seemed to coalesce around this fairly quickly. Even before Amodei published his blog post, I was seeing other people post some version of this [plan,] just in the days leading up to it. My understanding is, these suggestions that have come out of the AI safety community; these are things that have been percolating for a while. They’re not just things that [Amodei] thought up on his own. But it just seemed like a lot of people were kind of ready to embrace this and in some ways, [it’s] encouraging to see that there’s a consensus. But it also makes me a little skeptical that this would represent genuine, major steps towards a slowdown. Kirsten: First of all, consensus can be a good thing. Also, it can be the beginnings of forming a cartel. And so, let’s be clear [about] who we’re talking about here. We’re talking about frontier AI labs. and that’s specific and important. You did say a minute ago that the details aren’t really clear, but we do know that the general idea here is that independent third-party evaluators would come in that would work inside [companies] like Anthropic or OpenAI and monitor AI safety practices and incidents. But there is a lot of vagueness around that. Then there’s another proposal to have major AI companies in democratic countries coordinate on safety standards and limits. And then this international coordination piece. So those are the general ideas around this. I’ll also add that there’s been very considerable pushback from very specific people. And surprisingly, some people I didn’t think would push back on this. The obvious one, I guess, would be Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, who had some pretty choice words. I don’t know what either of you think of […] some of his comments and the call he took from President Trump onstage [at the All-In Summit]. Sean: I think Jensen understands that, to a certain extent, he is seen as the adult in the room here. Which is interesting, because that’s a dynamic that I think has changed.

events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt There is no dearth of different forms of hardware for meeting note-taking , including pendants, pins, and credit-card-styled devices. That hasn’t stopped Vocci from releasing a new device for the same use case in a ring form factor, which is convenient but could create some privacy issues. The ring form factor is one of the easiest for anyone who wants to just press a button and have the device start recording. Pebble’s new Index 01 Ring, which I am testing right now, lets you hold the button and take a note or a reminder. Stream Ring, made by Sandbar, works similarly with a control pad on the top. Vocci’s ring takes a different path, with meeting note-taking as a central function. The ring has a button, which you can double-tap to start recording and double-tap again to stop. You can tap and hold the button to ask Vocci AI questions, but that only works when you have the app open. There is an indicator light and a haptic motor for recording feedback. The ring is lightweight at under six grams and uses titanium material on the inner and outer surfaces — likely a coating. The company claims that the Vocci ring can record notes for eight hours on a single charge. The device comes with a chunky plastic case, which can charge the ring up to three times. The device captures meetings very well. I have had conversations spanning more than an hour in loud cafes, and the ring managed to convert most of the chat into accurate transcripts. However, this method of note-taking is not great if you want to take short notes. The software is the disappointing part of the Vocci ring. The app itself is a bit confusing. Whenever I took shorter notes, I saw AI-generated insights that were longer than the notes themselves. Each recording has Chat, which is the main transcript; Highlights, which are short snippets you can capture by pressing the button while recording a conversation; and Notes, which is a summary and insight of the whole conversation. In the app, there is a tab called Base where you can find transcripts, recordings, and anything you generate from them, and I found that redundant. I didn’t find a way to directly initiate a chat with AI for session transcripts. Voice-enabled rings are a great form factor for taking short notes or reminders. The app doesn’t have direct integration with reminder apps, which is a bummer. The feature rollout for its software is also slow. The company informed me that users can use Vocci’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to other assistants, but the option to do that didn’t appear until a few weeks ago in the app. Other meeting notetakers are building their platforms to allow users to automate insights and workflow through AI, and at the moment, Vocci’s platform is not fully built out for that. There are some privacy concerns with this device because of its form factor. Vocci’s ring looks like a regular piece of jewelry until someone notices the button on it. The ring has a recording indicator, but it faces the user. It’s best practice to let someone know that you are recording a conversation, and it’s also required by law in some countries and regions. But with this kind of device, some miscreants can easily choose not to disclose that information and record the conversation without anyone noticing. The company said it encourages people to disclose that they are recording, but that may not be enough. At $249, the ring is pricey compared to other note-takers like Plaud or Pocket , and that is due to the device’s lightweight form factor. The ring is for someone who doesn’t want to stick a gadget on the back of their phone, wear a wristband, or wear a pendant. On the hardware layer, a lot of these devices are combinations of some microphones, a battery, and a connection to the phone. We will likely see more variety in hardware meeting note-takers in the coming years, until users pick the specific formats that work for them. events.title: ScrollEd wants to turn textbooks into TikTok
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Society has spent a lot of time bemoaning our digitally addled minds and goldfish-like attention spans, pointing the finger of blame at doomscrolling as the reason we can’t just sit down and read a book or study for exams. But what if the solution isn’t to stop scrolling, but to rethink what we’re scrolling through? That’s the bet startup ScrollEd is making. The Palo Alto-based startup is pitching in the TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield 200 competition with the novel idea that if students won’t open a textbook, the textbook should open itself up to them — as a scroll. ScrollEd has built an app that allows the user to turn any text file — including dry PDFs or text books — into a feed that feels a lot like Instagram Reels or TikTok. As you scroll, the content shows up as AI-generated video, audio, text, or even interactive quizzes. Swiping up surfaces a new topic, while swiping sideways lets you go deeper into the one you’re on, with a quiz waiting for you at the end. “The younger generation is increasingly going short form, vertical feed only (especially the 18 year olds we’ve spoken to!), and this poses challenges for any kind of media that requires depth,” Utsav Gupta, ScrollEd’s co-founder, told TechCrunch in an email. “We want to meet them where they are…We just have to be deliberate about how we use it and choose not to maximize engagement on the platform.” “A short video can make you curious; following that curiosity can mean searching for another explanation or leaving the app,” Gupta continued. “We wanted going deeper to be as easy as moving to the next video.” Gupta bootstrapped ScrollEd this year alongside his co-founder and wife Rebecca Neff after the two both noticed feeling dissatisfied after doomscrolling before bed. Both are students — Gupta studies AI and human purpose at Stanford, and Neff studies computer science at the University of Pennsylvania. The startup is targeting educational institutions, corporate training programs, and individuals who “just want something better to scroll on,” according to Gupta. ScrollEd is following a freemium model, combining a free consumer feed with a paid ScrollEd Pro subscription and annual institutional licenses. Institutions pay to deliver educational material through the platform, in exchange for reports about engagement, lesson progress, and other data. In the coming months, ScrollEd intends to focus on its consumer launch, building its lesson library and source-checking workflow, and developing pilots for institutions. (The company will launch its consumer business at Disrupt, in fact. “We’re hoping to ‘disrupt’ social media and short form!” Gupta joked.) The startup is also building infrastructure that will one day allow educators to assess individual learners and adapt to their needs. “The ambition is a social network that’s better for you,” Gupta said. events.title: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is O n 8 September, OpenAI claimed that its AI agents had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous and difficult challenges in mathematics. Had a human solved it, they would have collected both prize money and plaudits from their fellows. The announcement instead ignited what some mathematicians have called an “ existential crisis ” in their field over the power of AI, and accusations that OpenAI misused human work . The maths behind Navier-Stokes is difficult to understand, but the critiques levelled by mathematicians will be familiar to artists, office workers, or anyone else concerned about AI. OpenAI’s results, like any arising from a large language model, depend on digesting work by human mathematicians. The OpenAI paper cites sources, but many believe the company didn’t give sufficient credit, especially to several mathematicians believed to be very close to a solution – bad form that erases human ingenuity and hogs all the glory. The mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also has concerns that work he was doing on Navier-Stokes using OpenAI’s Codex model was seen by the OpenAI team. OpenAI has denied directly accessing this material, but could not rule out that data from Buckmaster’s use of their products “helped improve our model”. This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many against the companies that develop these systems. It has yet to be adequately addressed. This is a particular misstep in the case of mathematics. As many mathematicians have pointed out, AI firms are keen to use their models’ maths prowess as an advertisement . But they rely on mathematicians to check their – often sloppy and baffling – work, and to tell them if it is useful and how it might be applied. An AI-produced movie or vaccine would have a clear and obvious use, whatever its merits, but it will take time and human intellectual labour to tell whether OpenAI’s purported solution contains any novel mathematical tools or insights. This should be an opportunity for collaboration. It has instead become yet another source of alienation and resentment. Despite this, mathematicians are remarkably open to the use of AI, even as they commit their names to open letters denouncing tech firms. Most recognise that the technology is undeniably powerful and particularly good at maths. There has been a nuanced discussion of how maths might change and integrate AI, with humans guiding and interpreting its work. There has also been some soul-searching as to whether celebrating the person – or machine – that achieved a flashy final result in the form of a mathematical proof is the best way to value contributions. As Bill Thurston, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, put it in 2010, well before the age of AI: “The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.” These are still uniquely human qualities. Some critics of AI are still stuck dismissing its outputs as uniformly useless “slop”. AI will not become good at everything. But more people may find themselves in the current position of mathematicians, confronted with the undeniable effectiveness of AI, while deeply concerned about how it is being used. This anxiety might not exist, the mathematician Nestor Guillen wrote recently, if we could separate the tech from the tech companies, and democratise its use. It is increasingly urgent that we find ways to do so.

The New York Times reports that California already required disclosure for influencers who post about state or local races — but when someone failed to disclose, there were no fines or criminal penalties. (Texas also requires disclosure for paid political content, and other states are considering similar regulations.) Under the new bill, AB 1130, regulators can fine influencers up to $5,000 for each violation, and they can also refer them to law enforcement for potential misdemeanors. According to the NYT, billionaire Tom Steyer, who unsuccessfully campaigned for the Democratic nomination for California governor earlier this year, paid dozens of influencers to post about his campaign online, and many of them did not initially disclose the payments. Newsom signed the legislation as part of a broader package of bills that his office said will protect against potential election interference from President Donald Trump. events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: How do we know when an AV is safe enough?
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! One of the stickier problems for autonomous vehicle developers, regulators, and the public is determining when self-driving technology is safe enough for the road. So far, that question has largely fallen to industry to answer — companies that are applying their autonomous vehicle technology to self-driving trucks, robotaxis, and maybe someday personally owned passenger vehicles. Today, there is no standardized test for judging how well an automated driving system performs in the real world. We require people to pass a driver’s test before getting a license, but there isn’t an equivalent test or system for autonomous vehicle technology. So how do we know whether an AV is a safe driver? The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s working on an answer. Federal motor vehicle safety standards (FMVSS) already govern the vehicle automakers sell today. But those FMVSS rules weren’t designed for vehicles like the Tesla Cybercab and Zoox robotaxi, which lack traditional, and federally required, equipment like pedals, steering wheels, and design features like side mirrors and rearview mirrors. The NHTSA is working on a federal automated vehicle framework that it says will put safety at the foundation without stifling innovation, or as Administrator Jonathan Morrison put it this week, force the agency to play “whack-a-mole” with policy decisions or try to predict how the technology will evolve. That’s a tricky recipe to get right. The agency took a notable step toward that goal this week by reaching an agreement with SAE to launch ASCEND, a government-industry initiative aimed at speeding up the development of data-driven AV performance standards. “Our top priority for this consortium is ADS competency, which will inform and accelerate a corresponding federal motor vehicle safety standard,” Morrison said at the AI Horizons Summit in Pittsburgh. “Ultimately, our ADS performance rulemaking will provide federal leadership in this space. By delivering an AV competency standard, we hope we’ll be able to address the burgeoning past patchwork of inconsistent state and local level requirements, and continue to encourage American innovation and promote the safe deployment and development of these vehicles on the road.” There is no timeline yet for when this consortium will produce ADS standards. But I bet the AV industry is already weighing in. Note: Want to hear Morrison’s complete comments? Check out this video of the AI Horizons Summit, and fast-forward to the 04:36:00 mark. We’re about to find out. Autonomous vehicle company May Mobility plans to go public through a merger with special purpose acquisition company ACP Holdings Acquisition Corp. in a deal that could raise more than $300 million at a valuation of $1.4 billion. There are other publicly traded companies working on autonomous vehicle technology: Aurora and Kodiak, which are both focused on self-driving trucks; Rivian; and Tesla. And while Waymo is not (yet) publicly traded, its parent company Alphabet is. It’s the same story for Amazon-owned Zoox. events.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
events.summary: Watch: Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey calls for immediate action on fuel costs Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living. The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January. Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze , deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year. The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump. Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy. "Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said. The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding." In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%. He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair. Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs. Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already. "Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them." Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out". Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty. "It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power. The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people. events.title: Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth
events.summary: Deputy leader Daisy Cooper says she has a plan for growth Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper has warned the UK's economic growth is being held back by a "computer says no" approach. She unveiled a 30-page growth plan , external aimed at removing barriers to business as part of her speech to the Lib Dem conference in Brighton. Cooper, who is also the party's Treasury spokesperson, said too many ideas, start-ups and research started in Britain but ended up being taken overseas. She also outlined a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU to reverse the economic damage of Brexit, that she claimed is currently costing the UK £90bn a year in lost tax revenue. Speaking on stage in Brighton, she said: "We build brilliant start-ups, and watch too many leave to scale somewhere else. We produce world-class research, and too little of it becomes a British product." "Britain has the potential," she went on. "The system holds it back. The computer says no. "This plan tears down the barriers to investment, to innovation, and to skills." Cooper called for the creation of a digital one-stop-shop service for businesses and investors, combining tax, regulatory, legal, Companies House, and general business services. Creating this within a new Department for Growth would simplify red tape and help small and medium-sized businesses compete and grow, she said. Cooper said a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU, would be the "single biggest growth lever we could pull" by deepening ties with Europe. "It could turbo-charge our economy and start to reverse the economic damage of Brexit which is currently costing us £90bn a year in lost tax revenue," she said. "In power, we will strike the deal on the single market, we will strike the deal on a customs union, we will strike the deal on defence." She claimed the Lib Dems would say "what no other party dares to say" that Britain "belongs at the heart of Europe, and we will take her there". Speaking to journalists after her speech, she added she believed re-joining the EU single market and customs union could be done "within a year". "We are very clear we want to join the single market and have a customs union and we think we can get there within a year," she said. Asked whether associate partnership could be an option for the UK, following the EU offer of a potential deal for Canada , she said: "I don't see why we need to wait - Canada is a long way away, the geography is different, it's a different relationship. "We are just a few miles away from the EU, our closest, biggest trading partner, we've got that historical relationship, we think we could get into the single market and have a customs union within 12 months." Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham said he would like to see the UK re-join the EU in his lifetime but he respected the result of the 2016 referendum and had no plans to "re-run" Brexit arguments . On Friday, Chancellor John Healey met EU ministers and asked them to let the UK into its Made in Europe scheme , aimed at protecting industries from unfair Chinese competition. Healey also pushed for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin the same day, as Burnham held his first official meeting with Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin in No 10 North. Seeking to differentiate the Liberal Democrats from rival parties, she said her party would avoid "more punishing tax hikes from Labour or painful spending cuts by the Conservatives and Reform UK". She attacked Healey for his speech earlier this month , which "contained no vision, no ideas, and absolutely no mention of Europe". Cooper also attacked Reform and the Conservatives for being "locked in a race to the bottom without a single credible costing between them". She highlighted how the new Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith had helped to deliver and defend the Liz Truss mini-budget, which she said "crashed the pound, it spiked your mortgage, it cost the country billions", and Nigel Farage defended the move. "But the worst could be yet to come: Farage is modelling himself on Trump," she said. "A President who has used the presidency to enrich himself, dismantled anti-corruption safeguards and pardoned crypto criminals. "We cannot allow that kind of politics to take hold in our country -- We cannot afford to allow Nigel Farage to win the keys to No 10 or let the Tories put him there." events.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
events.summary: Germany's electric car boom cuts fuel tax revenue The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure. "People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW bluntly. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway." According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year. Norway is leading the way , with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered cars in the country. The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%. The boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm in the German government, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes. Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 euro-cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 euro-cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax. With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club. The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite." "If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses. EU overturns combustion engine ban amid industry pressure According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year. In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050. "The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report stated. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, the report added. In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023. Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits. In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act. That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued. Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said. Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation. In the UK, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro-cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids. Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees. In Switzerland, meanwhile, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations. Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles , has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls. Why big automakers are losing China In Germany, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account. "The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster . "If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report. Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.

events.title: Bernie Sanders is right about the four-day workweek – but wrong about how to get there
events.summary: The senator proposed a federal overtime rule mandate, but incentives can better spur employers to reshape the workweek Bernie Sanders , the Vermont senator, recently proposed new legislation that would change federal overtime rules. The new law, if passed, would require employers to pay a minimum 1.5 hours of overtime for each hour worked past 32 hours in a week. Currently, overtime kicks in at 40 hours per week. The requirement would phase in over a few years. Sounds great. Who wouldn’t want that? There’s just one problem: somebody has to pay for it. For business owners, this isn’t an ideological argument. It’s math. Say a company employs 100 people. And, for argument’s sake, say that each employee earns $50,000 annually for a 40-hour workweek. Assuming 50 workweeks, that’s about $1,000 per week or $25 an hour. Under Sanders’ proposal that employee would make $25 per hour for the first 32 hours and then be paid overtime of time and a half, or $37.50 for the additional eight hours to make it a 40-hour workweek. Which means that for a full week the employer is now paying $1,100 per week or $55,000 per year for 50 weeks. That’s $5,000 more for each employee. And it’s actually more than that. You have to add in federal and state taxes that an employer pays – about 7% of wages, which adds $350 more per year. A small business that employs 25 people would then be paying an additional $133,750 more per year under Sanders’ proposal. If they had 50 employees it would be an added cost of $267,500 per year. Well, you can do the math from there. And I’m not including other benefits – retirement plan contributions, workers compensation, etc – that are usually calculated as a percentage of wages. These costs would also go up. Of course, the business doesn’t have to pay for a 40-hour week. They can limit the workweek to 32 hours. But with unemployment and open jobs at historically low levels, I encounter very few businesses that can do this. They can’t find enough employees to do the work they have. No business wants to be forced to pay more for fewer hours. Up until now, many business owners have been dabbling with AI. But the owner of a 50-person company would gladly spend $100,000 on an AI project to save $267,500 per year. Sanders wants a moratorium on AI development. But now he’s proposing a law which would give employers another financial incentive to automate. The CEOs of Microsoft, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI must love this. The solution, I believe, is to accept that the workplace has changed. Today’s workers value compensation in different ways. It’s not just an hourly wage or a weekly paycheck. Recent research suggests that additional time off can have psychological benefits that an equivalent cash bonus doesn’t provide. According to a recent study in the Journal of Managerial Psychology , a majority of employees favored getting more time off over extra compensation. Researchers found that “a vacation time benefit gave surveyed employees an internalized sense of being treated and valued as a complete human being”. Getting paid a livable wage is of course important. But many workers, particularly in the younger generations that make up more than half of today’s workforce – want something just as important: balance. They want flexibility. They want to spend more time with their families, traveling, relaxing and pursuing their own personal interests. Providing incentives to – not mandating – employers to provide more paid time off, dependent care leave, and sick and personal days would make more sense. The government already provides employer tax credits for providing family leave and other benefits for reimbursing dependent-care expenses. This is also a valuable form of compensation, and one that more accurately addresses the issues that today’s employees face. Which is why a 32-hour, or four-day, workweek isn’t a bad concept. Government can help, but in the end it’s employers who need to step up. A four-day workweek can be accommodated by better scheduling. I know nurses, veterinarians, and healthcare and construction workers who are employed by firms that offer their employees to work four 10-hour days and take three days off. They love it. Of course, some jobs may not be amenable to such a schedule, and other paid-time-off plans for those workers should be considered. But if an employer invests the time to come up with a strategy for allowing their employees to only come to work four days a week (while still meeting the requirements of their job), they’ll find it easier to attract and retain talent.

events.title: Value of goods through Sharjah-Oman logistics corridor jumps 66% in three months
events.summary: The value of goods transiting through Sharjah and Oman logistics corridor has jumped more than 66 per cent in the first three months of operations as shippers looks to avoid the turbulent Strait of Hormuz amid the continuing Iran war. Goods worth Dh1.7 billion ($463.21 million) have been traded since May 17, when the corridor was launched to allow shipments to cross borders seamlessly into the Sultanate’s ports. Launched by Sharjah Ports, Customs and Free Zones Authority with Oman Customs, the dedicated corridor reflects the success of an “integrated sea–land logistics model that supports smoother trade flows and improves supply chain efficiency”, Sharjah Customs said in a statement on Sunday. The initiative allows importers, exporters, freight companies and logistics service providers with “more flexible and competitive logistics solutions”, it added. With the Iran war now in its seventh month, the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global route that powers global commerce, remains effectively shut, with continued Iranian attacks on commercial shipping. The significantly reduced flow of vessels through the narrow waterway, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passed before the conflict, has also disrupted commodities trade and upended supply chains. To circumvent the strait, heavy goods vehicles are now used far more extensively in the UAE to collect everything from supermarket staples to industrial goods from Oman and Saudi Arabia, and send manufactured items out through Omani ports. Lorry movements through the logistics corridor surpassed 34,000, while processed customs declarations exceeded 32,000 during the first three months of operation. Connections The corridor connects cargo flows between ports and logistics hubs of Sharjah and Oman via the Khatmat Malaha Border Crossing in Kalba and Al Madam Border Crossing, extending into Oman. The connection allows businesses multiple options for moving goods, as well as shortening the end-to-end cargo journey, which also cuts cargo handling stages and improves the efficiency of logistics operations. The interconnection links Sharjah and other UAE ports with Sohar, Duqm and Salalah ports in Oman, opening “two complementary routes for cargo according to destination and logistics requirements”, Sharjah Customs said. “The early results recorded by the corridor during its first months of operation reflect the success of the vision underpinning the project,” Mohammed Al Raisi, director of Border Crossings and Entry Points Affairs at the Sharjah Ports, Customs and Free Zones Authority, said. “From the outset, our goal was to offer the business community far more than a mere transit route.” Al Raisi added that the growth in trade flows and customs transactions, coupled with new customers joining the ecosystem within a relatively short period, reflects rising demand for the integrated logistics solutions offered by the corridor.

events.title: Fed rate hike reflects new world of sticky inflation, faster growth
events.summary: Trump renewed his attacks on the Fed after it hiked its benchmark interest rate. WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump has renewed his attacks on the Federal Reserve after it hiked its benchmark interest rate Wednesday , but the Fed matters less than broader economic trends when it comes to longer-term borrowing costs, economists say. The economy is growing steadily despite being hit with repeated shocks — and may even be accelerating — while inflation remains stubbornly high . And big tech firms are borrowing huge amounts of cash to plow into data center construction while the federal government is still running large yearly budget deficits . All these trends point to higher interest rates regardless of what the Fed does, analysts say. As a result, the low interest-rate, low-inflation world that lasted for nearly 15 years after the Great Recession is over and a higher-priced, higher-rate world is taking its place. Mortgage rates fell into the 3% range in the 2010s and even lower during COVID-19, but such deals are long gone. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached 6.95% last week , the highest in more than a year and a half. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax consulting firm, said that a big reason for the change is a shift from the pre-pandemic economy in which consumer and business demand was weak, to the current economy in which healthy consumer and business spending is colliding with supply shocks and bottlenecks. In addition to higher oil and gas prices because of the Iran war, the AI buildout has struggled with an insufficient supply of computer chips, electronic equipment, and workers to put it all together. “We’ve undergone a structural transformation of the economy,” Brusuelas said. “The regime change in inflation and interest rates is the outcome.” The shift, in many ways, returns the economy to where it was before the financial crisis in December 2007 that lasted through June 2009. But even after the downturn ended, consumer and business spending remained weak. Millions of Americans in the 2010s focused on paying down outsized mortgages and credit card debt instead. Businesses saw few investment opportunities, and many big tech firms such as Alphabet’s Google and Meta’s Facebook piled up cash. Now those companies are using those stockpiles to build out AI data centers, and are borrowing even more money to do so. And American consumers — despite surveys finding they are pessimistic about the economy — are still spending at a healthy pace. A recent report showing that retail sales picked up last month led economists at Bank of America to forecast growth will reach a healthy 3% at an annual rate in the July-September quarter. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh highlighted the shift in a speech at the central bank's annual conference in Jackson Hole, Wyoming last month. After 2008, “it was a widely held view that an excess of capital would sit on the sidelines for a long, long time, because there just wouldn’t be enough compelling investment opportunities,” Warsh said. “All the good stuff had been invented. So growth would be low and slow. “Well, times sure have changed,” he continued. “Ever-expanding pools of capital are pouring into AI-related infrastructure of all sorts.” Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber dies at 27 Hunter charged with manslaughter in shooting of woman he mistook for a deer: Police Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital The additional spending and investment has contributed to higher longer-term interest rates on government bonds that are competing for lenders. The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond topped 5% this year for the first time since 2023, even before the Fed raised its benchmark short-term rate Wednesday. At the same time, political polling and consumer sentiment surveys continue to find that many Americans are struggling to keep up with rising prices, and affordability remains a top concern heading into the midterm elections. Even as the economy expands, inflation has outpaced the annual growth in average wages for the past five months. Brusuelas said the U.S. economy's expansion is “imbalanced” with growth “entirely dependent” on the AI buildout and strong spending by wealthier consumers, who have benefited from rising stock prices driven by hopes that AI will lift profits. After the Fed lifted its rate to 3.9% Wednesday, Trump said on Truth Social that U.S. rates should be 1% instead. Yet many of Trump's policies have contributed to higher borrowing costs, in particular the Iran war that has driven up gas prices. When inflation persists, investors demand higher interest rates on longer-term Treasury bonds, such as the 10-year, which strongly influences mortgage rates.

events.title: UK startup snares $20m to recreate gigs with ‘hyper-realistic’ digital avatars
events.summary: Unit1 hopes to offer lower cost version of shows such as Abba Voyage, showcasing living and dead artists in any venue The former chief executive of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s entertainment group has obtained a near-£15m investment for his UK music tech startup that hopes to recreate classic concerts by manifesting musicians as digital avatars. Unit1 was set up last year by Barney Wragg, an entertainment executive who ran Lord Lloyd-Webber’s Cats-to-Evita empire for five years from late 2011. It has secured the $20m in funding from a group of investors, including tech backer Balderton Capital through its partner Daniel Waterhouse, who made early investments in Spotify. The company hopes to stage concerts fronted by the “hyper realistic” digital avatars of living artists who are no longer touring and by recreating existing performances from dead musicians. In the latter case, it will develop the avatars through a mixture of archive footage and hiring actors and musicians who either look or play like the departed star, before blending the footage together. Unit1 has tested the technology with Scottish singer-songwriter and musician KT Tunstall , who worked with Wragg during a stint at the music company EMI. In the pilot, Tunstall was filmed in a London studio by motion capture cameras as she recreated a two-decade-old performance on Later… with Jools Holland, using the avatar to update her features to the way she looks now. The music industry has long flirted with the idea of creating avatars of its biggest stars, such as the 2012 hologram projection of the late rapper Tupac Shakur alongside Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre at Coachella festival. The concept found mainstream success with the 2022 launch of Abba Voyage, a lucrative virtual concert with avatars of the Swedish pop group, which runs in a purpose-built venue in east London. Unit1 hopes to offer a lower cost to produce version of the Abba Voyage experience, by providing artists, venues, their rights holders and promoters with a route to digital shows without needing a dedicated space. The setup also means a show could in theory tour in several countries simultaneously. The business will invest the fresh funds into research and development, as well as securing intellectual property and licensing deals with artists and their estates. Unit1’s aim is to stage shows with real musicians playing live instruments on stage alongside digital performers. The audience will view a high-definition LED screen, which is combined with extra lights, sound and props to give them the illusion they are watching a fully human performance. “For the audience member in the room it is seamless between the digital and the physical room, immersing them,” Wragg told the Guardian. “It’s a teleportation of an audience member to a time and place.” However, some fans have expressed unease about dead musicians being digitally resurrected. Earlier this year, a plan to create a lifesize AI-powered avatar of the late Black Sabbath frontman Ozzy Osbourne was criticised as being disrespectful and in poor taste by some fans. Wragg said that, in most cases, the startup was “dealing with family members of estates to create something which is well documented and understood – extremely well-known concerts or live recordings. We are mindful that you do not want to be distasteful.” He was tight-lipped on which classic concerts Unit1 could recreate. He has previously said he wished he could have seen various well-known performances, including Queen at Live Aid, the Beatles’ performances at the Cavern Club and Jimi Hendrix at Woodstock. Balderton – which has also backed music rights firm Kobalt and fintech Revolut – was joined in the funding round by its existing investors, including the venture capital firm Mercuri and Paul McGuinness, the Irish music executive who managed U2 from the late 1970s until 2013.

events.title: Three Republican power players walk into a D.C. bar, and ...
events.summary: It sounds like the start of an only-in-D.C. joke: Three Republican power players walk into a bar for a freewheeling conversation. They unwittingly sit next to a liberal comic. She then skewers them in an Instagram post recounting their chat. Why it matters: It became no laughing matter for one of the Republicans —oilman Harry Sargeant — who's trying to improve his uneasy relations with the Trump administration, partly related to his business dealings in Venezuela . His rapprochement efforts were complicated last month when senior administration officials became aware of the comic's social media post, in which she alleged that Sargeant spoke negatively about President Trump. The big picture: The story illustrates the panopticon of modern society and, especially, the nation's capital. Everyone is watched and being watched. And the White House takes notes on who's naughty and nice to Trump. Zoom in: The episode unfolded Aug. 18 in the Bourbon Lounge of the Four Seasons hotel in D.C., where comic Suzanne Lambert was working on jokes for an upcoming set, she said in a post to her 495,000 Instagram followers that had 2 million views before she took it down. In the video, Lambert said she coincidentally wound up sitting next to Sargeant and noted a vibe shift when two other men walked in: Pete Marocco and Gentry Beach. Marocco was described by Fox News as the "mastermind" who helped dismantle USAID early in the second Trump administration. Politico subsequently reported he had tensions with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Beach was the subject of a Wall Street Journal profile last year about how the lobbyist name-drops his longtime friend and presidential son Donald Trump Jr., in international business affairs, including one involving a Russian oil deal. Inside the room: Lambert said her in post that she was just "minding my business" but started to pay more attention when the men at the bar began "spouting off about Trump. I hear Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump." At one point, Lambert's post attributed comments to Sargeant that allegedly disparaged Trump and Republicans' midterm chances. Sargeant, through his attorneys, vigorously disputes that. Behind the scenes: Lambert's video quickly went viral, prompting Sargeant's attorneys to send her a cease and desist letter. Lambert took the post down but by then, the post had circulated among Trump advisers. Rubio was made aware of it, a source said. "Harry's got some problems, and what the White House saw didn't help," an administration source said of Sargeant. What they're saying: "Mr. Sargeant denies categorically the false statements attributed to him by a self-proclaimed liberal content creator and, as a patriot who served his country well as a Marine fighter pilot, supports fully President Trump's vision, leadership and tireless efforts to place America first," his attorney, Jason Wright, said in a written statement. Beach and Marocco declined to comment through Wright. A Lambert spokesperson didn't return emails. The intrigue: Sargeant first developed a challenging relationship with Rubio back in Florida, beginning in 2010. At the time, Rubio successfully ran for U.S. Senate against former Gov. Charlie Crist. Sargeant's is a friend and former Florida State University fraternity brother of Crist's who helped finance the ex-governor's campaign. Sargeant's oil business dealings with former Venezuelan strongman Nicolas Maduro, whom Rubio loathes, did little to improve their relations through the years. After Trump returned to the presidency last year, Rubio was appointed secretary of state and pushed for regime change in Caracas. Sargeant's ally, Trump special envoy Richard Grenell, was initially opposed . Rubio won out. U.S. forces seized Maduro in a raid on Jan. 3. A month later, after a Wall Street Journal article about Sargeant's involvement in Venezuela after Maduro was gone, Trump singled him out in a Truth Social post that said Sargeant "has no authority, in any way, shape, or form, to act on behalf of the United States of America, nor does anyone else that is not approved by the State Department." On Aug. 7, the Treasury Department sanctioned one of Sargeant's companies and froze its assets. He had divested its interests, for $300 million, to North American Blue Energy Partners, called NABEP. 11 days later, Sargeant wound up at the Four Seasons bar with Marocco and Beach (and Lambert). Nine days after that, NABEP became the vehicle for Trump's mammoth Venezuelan oil deal, which Axios first reported on Aug. 27. Zoom out: Trumpworld insiders say Sargeant's ordeal is a cautionary tale to stay on the good side of the administration. "I don't like Harry, but he got knifed," said one Trump adviser. "They kick him out of Venezuela. They sanction his company. They take him out of this other deal. And some people want him investigated ." A former business associate of Sargeant's pointed out that he financially supported Trump's campaign in 2020 and, at the time, even played a role in helping Trump push to have Ukraine investigate Joe Biden, "Harry wasn't disloyal to Trump," the associate said. "He's an oil guy. He wants to do oil deals. And he should've just gone with Team Rubio from the start."

events.title: The tech battle to build your AI assistant
events.summary: The long-promised personal AI assistant is finally arriving, with a suddenly crowded field of agents offering to run pieces of your everyday life. Why it matters: For years, tech's "personal assistants" were little more than voice-controlled search boxes. Rapid advances in AI are finally giving them the memory, judgment and autonomy to act on our behalf. Catch up fast: Chatbots answer questions. AI agents can actually do things — shopping, making calls, booking tickets, managing calendars and navigating the web. The model first took off in coding and other professional work. Now it's spilling into the far more intimate terrain of everyday life. The intrigue: OpenAI is expected to enter the market soon after hiring the creator of OpenClaw — a breakout hit among AI power users earlier this year — to "drive the next generation of personal agents." Driving the news: A consumer-agent race has erupted almost overnight, with startups and tech giants pursuing the same basic idea — persistent digital proxies that know your life. Instinct has become buzzy by connecting to users' email, messages, screen, audio and location — then proactively texting or calling to help run their lives. It recently added its own email addresses and the ability to make phone calls, and is now in talks for a $10 billion valuation . Grok Bot, launched by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI in August, gives persistent agents their own cloud computers, lets them sign into users' apps and keeps them working around the clock. Meta's Muse brought the concept to a broader consumer audience this month with a polished app, a customizable avatar and deep integration with Meta's ecosystem. Apple's Siri is finally getting its AI overhaul , bringing more context and capability to an assistant already built into hundreds of millions of devices. The big picture: The battle to become your personal agent is also a battle to become the keeper of your personal information and data. The frontier AI race has revolved around raw intelligence. Personal agents win by becoming useful and deeply embedded in your daily life. The more an agent knows about your relationships, schedule and spending, the more useful it becomes. Between the lines: Becoming someone's default agent could be one of the most valuable relationships in consumer technology. People are likely to share far more with an AI that manages their lives than they did with a search engine. The catch: Nobody yet knows what price consumers will pay for that convenience, in cost or privacy. Apple says some server-based Apple Intelligence features, including the upgraded Siri, will have usage limits , with expanded access potentially tied to iCloud plans. Meta is offering free and paid Muse tiers, while pitching the product as more privacy-conscious than its earlier AI offerings. What to watch: Some people inside and outside the industry argue that users should own the personal data and context their agents accumulate, rather than handing that relationship to ad-driven tech giants. will.i.am, whose FYI.AI offers agents equipped with their own phone numbers that can text, call and collaborate with humans to build projects, says he recoils at getting an agent for free "in exchange for extracting your very core — how you think." "That's nasty," the Black Eyed Peas frontman told Axios. "We've seen that with social media."

events.title: Trump's proposed Washington arch to become sniper, drone facility
events.summary: President Trump said Sunday morning his proposed " triumphal arch " in Washington, D.C., will become a dual-use facility housing snipers, drones and ammunition storage. Why it matters: The president is now framing construction of the arch as a national security issue — much like he did with the East Wing ballroom /military complex at the White House. What they're saying: "At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch , planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," Trump posted on Truth Social. Catch up quick: The proposed 250-foot arch would be one of the largest such monuments in the world, sparking concerns that it could interfere with other national symbols, block views and even complicate landings for pilots at nearby airports. The New York Times reported this week that the National Park Service is rushing through a final review of the project ahead of a likely approval in November. The NPS's own August report indicated the construction of the arch would have adverse effects on many nearby monuments and landmarks. This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
