events.title: Civic life starts close to home and leads to the ballot box
events.summary: The system isn’t perfect. But we all have a say—in the places we gather, the communities we build, and the future we share. Civic participation doesn’t begin at the ballot box. It starts with learning to listen to different perspectives right where you are. That means building the skills to participate in civic life—learning how communities work together, navigating the swirl of election information, and heading to the polls to vote. For Dave Leichtman, community involvement was a family tradition. The director of global elections at Microsoft remembers riding in his grandfather’s truck as a kid—climbing steep hills and canvassing farm to farm to build support for a new water district in rural Oklahoma. “My grandfather was honest with our neighbors. He said there would be piped water, but their taxes would go up,” Leichtman recalls. “He’d shake hands, look people in the eye, and tell them what he was proposing.” Today, Leichtman carries those lessons forward to his daughters, discussing candidates and ballot measures with them well before Election Day. That commitment extends across Microsoft, where thousands of employees organize in support of National Voter Registration Day. Microsoft’s voter registration initiative picked up steam in 2019 and has since become a cornerstone of Microsoft’s Societal Resilience work—supporting civic engagement, safe and secure elections, and healthy information ecosystems. As millions of Americans prepare to weigh in on congressional, state, and local races on November 3, Leichtman reminds everyone: “Make a plan. Know how you’re going to vote. Know what you need to vote. Know the deadlines.” Leichtman constantly encourages people to get involved in their communities and work alongside their neighbors. Microsoft employees are already answering the call, volunteering with the League of Women Voters , VoteRiders , and dozens of other civic organizations to help get out the vote. That spirit of participation inspired the virtual world of Village Square, a new game-based learning experience that began when the Tech for Society team approached Minecraft Education about collaborating with iCivics . Through gameplay, students explore the foundations of civic engagement—balancing competing community needs, making collective decisions, and seeing how every voice shapes the outcome. Lisa Reppell, senior program manager for information literacy, knew she had found her path when she attended her first community town hall in 2001. Held at a Boise public library, the discussion centered on the Patriot Act and the tensions between civil liberties and national security. “Those are two deeply important values that require debate in the public square,” she recalls. She now leads information literacy on the Elections and Societal Resilience Team at Microsoft—and that includes AI, increasingly a front door to election information. Reppell’s team is preparing to launch a voter education initiative ahead of the midterms: Check. Recheck. Vote. Originally launched in 2024 to help voters recognize risks posed by deepfakes, or deceptive AI-generated content, this year’s campaign focuses on practical AI literacy. She says, “We’re really trying to respond to the reality that AI is starting to change the way that people are finding information about the election—whether people are going to an AI chatbot or doing their same old internet search but with an AI-generated summary.” Check. Recheck. Vote. encourages voters to check sources and citations behind an AI-generated answer, recheck by visiting those sources and comparing what other credible sources say, and vote using official information. Reppell is encouraged to see that more voters are using AI to deliberately understand the candidates and issues on their ballots. “AI can clarify information and compare the data sources you bring to it, but it shouldn’t tell you who to vote for,” she says. “AI can’t make your judgments for you.” Rylin Rodgers, director of global disability policy at Microsoft, says she was born for her role. Born in 1975—the year the U.S. guaranteed disabled students the right to a free appropriate public education —she was among the first generation of children to arrive at kindergarten with an individualized education program. Rodgers may not have known at five that her experience in Bellevue, WA was an outcome of public policy and advocacy, but over time, the connection became clear. “As a disabled woman, I really understand what policy does in terms of access.” To keep elections accessible, Rodgers advocates designing systems with every voter in mind. She uses the example of curb cuts, which serve wheelchair users, as well as parents with strollers and people pushing shopping carts. Similarly, a polling place designed for someone who is blind or has low vision may also help an older adult or someone who forgot their glasses. “When we design something well, it works better for all of us,” she says. Putting that principle into action, Microsoft has partnered with the International Foundation for Electoral Systems to develop Election PATHS , a living database of election technologies and accessibility features. Drawing on information from tech providers and disability-rights advocates around the world, it equips election officials to make informed purchasing decisions. A related resource, the Accessible Democracy Tracker, measures voting-access barriers and opportunities at polling places nationwide. Civic participation depends on people showing up. Not because everyone agrees. Not because every system is perfect. But because the communities we live in—and the future we share—are shaped by the people who choose to take part. “It’s so easy to get involved locally. Go serve on a board or committee for the county or the schools that are not filled,” Leichtman urges. And the easiest way to stay civically engaged is to vote. He says, “You’ve got all this energy. You want to advocate for the things you care about. You want your voice to be heard. Take it to the ballot.” Finding the next question with Trevor Noah Going the distance Future of society A community’s resilience against cybersecurity threats. events.title: Anthropic decides to support OpenAI's markdown instructions spec
events.summary: Anthropic on Friday surprised the developer community by supporting rival OpenAI's mechanism for passing marching orders to AI agents. This makes life easier for folks who use both platforms. "We're adding support for AGENTS.md to Claude Code," said Claude Code engineer Thariq Shihipar in a social media post. "Starting today in version 2.1.277, if there is no CLAUDE.md in a folder, Claude will check for and use AGENTS.md." Claude Code users can toggle this behavior, he said, with the /config command. Until now, developers who use Claude Code alongside OpenAI Codex or other non-Anthropic tools have had to maintain two sets of Markdown instructions for their AI agents: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, not to mention project-specific versions of these files. These documents get read by coding agents with every request. They outline expected behavior, preferred tool usage, coding conventions, and so on. They lay the foundation of the agent's context. The two formats are similar but not identical – CLAUDE.md may contain Claude-specific instructions while AGENTS.md is intended to be tool agnostic. Because these documents can change, those working with AI agents have implemented various workarounds, like creating symlinks to keep CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in sync. Last year, OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md to the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation, in a bid to build support for its standard. As of December 2025, more than 60,000 open source projects implemented AGENTS.md. The popularity of Claude Code has given Anthropic the latitude to insist on its own standards, but it appears the company has decided there's nothing to be gained from continued specification separatism. For those who use AI coding tools, this detente is an event of modest significance. Many widely followed software developers applauded the decision in social media posts. Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI's head of core product, remarked, "Yay! This is the way. Come to the light," to which Shihipar responded with the handshake emoji (🤝). It's enough to bring a tear to the eye. ®

events.title: Health wonks question who saves in Trump drug program
events.summary: President Trump took a victory lap on his administration’s work on drug pricing today, announcing all 50 states will participate in the “most-favored-nation” program, saying “this one thing alone should win us the midterms.” But health policy experts question whether the changes will directly save consumers money, and for how long. The White House estimates federal and state governments will save $64.3 billion from most-favored-nation pricing, but experts say that won’t necessarily change the price Medicaid beneficiaries pay for their medicines. “It’s worth being super-explicit: If you are a Medicaid patient, these drugs are already cheap. GENEROUS is not going to make medicines more affordable,” said Brian Reid, principal at health consultancy Reid Strategic, referring to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services program. “The best-case scenario is that there is a small benefit to the Medicaid programs themselves. But I haven’t seen anyone suggest that this would make a whit of difference for patients.” There are also other outstanding questions such as which specific drugs are included in the effort and which states will take the pricing for which drugs. Peter Maybarduk, Access to Medicines director for Public Citizen, also said the Trump administration’s 10-year estimate is questionable, in part because the confidential drug pricing deals could remain in place only through the end of Trump’s term. — David Lim

events.title: USPS made mail slower to cut costs. Midterm ballots will test the system.
events.summary: The U.S. Postal Service has slowed down mail deliveries so much it's failing to meet even its lowered performance targets, a new report from the Government Accountability Office found. Why it matters: The Postal Service is part of the connective tissue of American life: delivering prescription drugs and ballots , carrying government notices and bills, helping businesses reach customers across the country. Now its attempts to shore up its finances are disproportionately affecting rural communities . The big picture: The Postal Service has given itself more time to deliver some first-class mail, the congressional watchdog's report notes, which millions of Americans rely on for medications, bills, paychecks, financial documents and mail-in ballots. The USPS is expected to fund itself largely through postage and other revenue while also providing universal service to nearly every U.S. address, even where doing so isn't profitable. By the numbers: The USPS added one to two days to expected delivery times for some mail after shifting some transportation from air to ground in 2021. The report said about 24,000 post offices will lose afternoon mail collection if they're more than 50 miles from a regional processing and delivery center, disproportionately affecting rural Americans. The intrigue: The service concerns come just weeks before the midterms, when millions of voters will rely on USPS to return ballots under state-specific deadlines. The Trump administration has pushed to dramatically overhaul the country's mail-in ballot system . What they're saying: "Whenever the post office closes … for rural communities, that takes the heart out of the place," Steve Hutkins, editor of Save the Post Office, tells Axios. "Everybody talks about how slow the mail is now. … The goalposts have moved several times," he said, adding that delivery times have slowed four times since 2010. "It all adds up." "The problem is if you want to cut costs to try to balance the books, you're going to cut services one way or another, and services usually means how fast the mail is moving, or whether there's a post office in your town." Case in point: Residents of one Phoenix neighborhood told Axios they sometimes went days or weeks without mail, leading to missed bills, checks and wedding invitations. Zoom in: Mark Jamison, a former postmaster in a small North Carolina town, tells Axios, says the decades-long push to operate the Post Office like a business has come at the expense of delivery service. "[I]n the age of ecommerce," he said, the Postal service acts "as a hedge against the delivery monopolies of UPS, FedEx, and Amazon." "The failure to understand the postal system as an essential infrastructure while trying to cram it into an ill-fitting, profit oriented, corporate model has caused serious damage to the infrastructure and been a great disservice to the American people." The other side: A USPS spokesperson pointed Axios to the agency's comments in the GAO report. "The Postal Service is well positioned to close the fiscal year strong, meet our higher target for first class mail on-time performance, and enter FY27 with significant momentum to set us up for a strong holiday mailing and shipping season." What we're watching: The GAO recommended the postmaster general explain how the agency plans to improve in its 2027 strategic plan update — and the office agreed. events.title: Microsoft agentically ports Copilot runtime to Rust for $120K
events.summary: The software engine underpinning GitHub Copilot and a growing number of Microsoft products is now written entirely in Rust, with AI agents doing most of the porting work. The migration cost about $120,000 in AI token usage plus about three weeks of a developer's time. However, managers also had to grapple with a few dozen regressions in the resulting code, pointing to AI’s ongoing challenges in understanding Rust. The effort updated the runtime module-by-module until the job was completed, spanning over 135 releases across a 14.5-week time period. Roughly 1.3 port pull requests were opened per day. Overall, agents converted 430,000 lines of TypeScript into 800,000 lines of production Rust. To keep the port as simple as possible, the port only replaced TypeScript modules on a case-by-case basis. It didn’t look to optimize the structure of the runtime itself. That work is next. And Rust, known for its lean performance, did not disappoint. One benchmark measured how quickly the runtime could complete 1,000 one-turn session lifecycles, using a shared client and 100 concurrent pipelines. The original TypeScript implementation completed 7.55 of those lifecycles per second, while Rust running in-process managed 120 per second - representing a 15.9x speedup on that particular workload. In terms of memory, a 10-client batch of agents consumed 1,383 MB with TypeScript while the Rust rewrite consumed only 126 MB serving the same swarm. Within Rust, the work remained in-process instead of spawning external background processes for completion, a requirement for TypeScript. Copilot from VS Code to Microsoft Office At first glance, most users may not know how pervasive the Copilot runtime is. It backs the GitHub Copilot command-line interface (CLI), the Copilot app, the SDK and the GitHub Copilot cloud agent. It shows up in VS Code, Visual Studio, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, and innumerable other Microsoft cloud services. Originally, the runtime was written in TypeScript and used Node.js as the framework and V8 for the execution engine. TypeScript and Node were ace for rapid development, but when used at scale, they suffered in terms of providing fast start-up and server density. “This is in no way a claim that every large TypeScript program should become Rust. Our requirements emphasized embedding through a C ABI, low startup and steady-state overhead, and predictable resource use. Rust made those goals possible,” wrote Microsoft Distinguished Engineer Stephen Toub in a post that explained the entire process. The project used Copilot to rewrite Copilot, which in turn used several LLMs – GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8 were both namechecked – to execute different parts of the job, depending on each LLM’s natural strength. Well-read but chatty agents Toub assessed the use of agents as largely successful. Indeed, this project would have taken years and cost millions if done by hand. Agents showed several surprising emergent behaviors, Toub noted. For one, they spent far more time gathering information than actually writing code. “The popular image of AI spewing code is almost backwards; at this scale, the work looked much more like iterative investigation, inspecting the current state, forming a hypothesis, making a targeted change, rinsing and repeating,” he wrote. Another surprise was how frequently sessions interacted with other sessions, either those they spawned or other ones entirely. One of the thorniest conversions was the session.ts file, which was over 30,000 lines of TypeScript that touched all aspects of the runtime. The porting session, which ended up taking 25 hours to complete, began by spending 56 minutes reading the documentation and making 122 tool calls for clarification. It then spawned 15 child sessions, each creating its own worktree and agent. Then, they started communicating with each other. Using a built-in orchestration skill, one session found every other active session and sent messages to those whose missions overlapped, requesting coordination. The compiler is a teacher, not an oracle Given its performance benefits, Rust has proven to be a popular language for rewriting applications. Bun creator Jarred Sumner, for instance, recently ported the Anthropic-owned JavaScript runtime and toolkit, which contained roughly 535,000 lines of Zig code, over to Rust, almost entirely using Claude agents. As of July 30, the experimental Rust port was passing 99.8 percent of Bun's existing tests on Linux x64 glibc, with the stable releases still shipping from the Zig codebase. That job cost $165,000 in tokens. But there are hidden dangers in using Rust as well, as Toub has found. For an LLM and a lazy programmer alike, if the code compiles, then it is valid Rust. But throughout the process, the project encountered dozens of regressions within the code. A regression is something that used to work, but no longer does after an update. The compiler has no idea, for instance, whether functions are in the right order, whether the job completes at an acceptable cost, whether it meets the developer's unwritten requirements, or whether it is internally coherent at all, for that matter. At RustConf, held in Montréal last week, consultant Lisa Crossman warned about the practice of treating the compiler as an “oracle,” or the last word on whether some Rust code is valid or not. “Rust stops the agent writing memory unsafe code; it does not stop the agent writing the wrong program correctly,” she said. If they’re wise, a human developer treats the compiler as a teacher, decoding the errors as a path to a better understanding of the language’s domain. An LLM, on the other hand, just uses the compiler as a black box, one it can batter with blunt, inefficient workarounds until one passes muster (perhaps this is what Zig creator Andrew Kelley meant when he called Bun’s Rust code “unreviewed slop”). In Toub’s case, he had found that compiler-approved regressions could come from ambiguous semantics and behaviors, branch drift, missing features that weren’t ported over, and differing behaviors from the replacement code. “That’s in no way an argument against Rust’s compiler,” Toub wrote. “But ‘if it compiles, it’s correct’ is useful only as a joke.” ®

events.title: 2028 Democrats like Newsom and Pritzker lean in on AI safety as Washington stalls
events.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a presumptive presidential candidate, is getting louder on AI, releasing an executive order amid the Washington stalemate. Why it matters: Democrats with national profiles this week are seizing on AI alarm, making their positions clear and Newsom – despite some deference shown to other 2028 contender Kamala Harris – wasn't going to sit this one out. Driving the news: Newsom on Friday issued an executive order tackling two major topics of debate inside the beltway this week -- independent auditors and kill switches. He did so taking direct aim at Washington: "With Donald Trump and Congress asleep at the wheel, Governor Gavin Newsom is once again taking the lead to strengthen AI safety for all Americans." Newsom was early to stake out a position on an issue that is increasingly politically salient, signing the first AI executive order in 2023. Between the lines: In the absence of U.S. legislation or more action from the Trump administration, states have stepped in to fill the void on AI regulation, a development some top AI execs sought to avoid. There are more than 600 bills in 47 states about AI, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, up 24% from last year. California, Illinois and Massachusetts are among the states leading the charge. All three are run by Democrats, who are seeking to seize the mantle of AI regulation nationally. Yes, but : Politicians in both parties are using antipathy toward data centers to punish opponents, including GOP candidates in gubernatorial races in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. California has emerged as both the state filling the federal regulatory void and one largely aligned with the frontier AI labs it is regulating. The executive order accelerates the implementation of two bills signed into law last week -- both of which were endorsed by OpenAI and Anthropic -- on independent verification organizations. Newsom's position on a kill switch is also aligned with what frontier labs are already working toward . The big picture: Former Vice President Harris this week also called for slowing down advanced AI development and Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker -- another presidential contender -- on Friday touted his AI bill . "Trump says that the only AI guardrails that we need are a strong and smart president. And, of course, he is neither of those things," Pritzker said. The Illinois bill requires companies to implement their own frameworks for frontier AI safety. A third party then has to create an annual report assessing whether developers are complying with that requirement. What we're watching: The Senate bill in Massachusetts goes further than Illinois, mandating independent evaluations of the models themselves, every four months. Anthropic has backed it , while OpenAI has backed a narrower version. OpenAI shifted its position on California's bills last week and may do so again in Massachusetts as AI alarm mounts.

events.title: Virginia governor wakes up to fact datacenters have become political cancer
events.summary: Virginia is not just for lovers, but is also for datacenters, hosting more than anywhere else in the world. However, the growth could be slowing as Governor Abigail Spanberger issued an executive order on Friday cracking down on bit barn builds in the state. “In the years before I took office, datacenters came to Virginia and the Commonwealth did not have a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians … That changes today,” Spanberger said in a statement. The executive order is part of a broader datacenter accountability framework that calls for greater transparency, a ban on nondisclosure agreements, limits on permitting, and more stringent environmental controls. Spanberger argues that existing policy lacked the precision necessary to hold bit barn builders accountable, and that the order is necessary to protect residents. In addition to greater transparency, the broader framework would require local approval for datacenters exceeding 25 megawatts and remove future large datacenters from the expedited permitting process, while the order calls on government officials to establish criteria to distinguish between responsible datacenter developments and those that would negatively impact residents or the environment. Speaking of the environment, the order would limit the use of water-intensive cooling towers in areas suffering from water scarcity, and encourage datacenter operators to either retrofit existing backup generators to reduce emissions or switch to battery storage, fuel cells, and other clean energy sources. Friday's order comes just days after the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors backed a plan to pause final action on certain new datacenter and substation applications for up to 12 months. Loudoun County is home to one of the highest concentrations of datacenters in the state. Opposition to datacenter development across the US is on the rise amid growing concerns over the server farms' impact on air quality, noise pollution, water use, and residents' electric bills. In Tennessee, Elon Musk's Colossus 2 datacenter is powered in part by 27 gas turbines across the state line in Mississippi, which are now the subject of an NAACP lawsuit alleging violations of the Clean Air Act. Meanwhile, some states have gone even further and outright blocked the development of new datacenters while local governments get a better handle on their potential impacts. In July, New York became the first state to temporarily halt datacenter buildouts exceeding 50 megawatts as part of an executive order signed by Governor Kathy Hochul. A month later, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro issued an executive order blocking datacenter permit applications unless they made legally binding commitments to abide by the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) requirements. Much like Virginia’s executive order, these rules seek to ensure residents don’t end up footing the bill for grid improvements built based on speculative demand. ®

events.title: GOP's Latino gains fade as deeper gender and generational divides emerge
events.summary: Latino voters swung sharply toward Republicans in 2024. Now, much of that gain is fading as gender and generational divides widen. Why it matters: The GOP breakthrough two years ago hasn't produced a uniformly more conservative Latino electorate, as Democrats have regained ground in polling this year. But an Axios analysis of recent polls shows Latino voters aren't simply swinging right, then left. The data show Latino politics fragmenting from within, as young Latino men and women increasingly split over immigration, President Trump and democracy. By the numbers: Democrats lead Republicans 56%-29% on the generic House ballot among 1,353 Latino registered voters in seven battleground states, according to a new bipartisan BSP Research/Shaw & Co. poll for the American Business Immigration Coalition and American Families United. Among Latino voters, Democrats lead in six states: Arizona, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas. Florida breaks the pattern, with Republicans holding a 44%-43% edge. The pollsters calculated that Democrats' advantage among Latinos is 11 points wider than their Latino margin in 2024. Neither party escapes voter dissatisfaction: 39% view congressional Democrats unfavorably, compared with 63% unfavorably for congressional Republicans. State of play: Inflation and gas prices remain voters' biggest concerns, but immigration remains highly salient — though voters don't choose between enforcement and legalization as an either-or. 63% called the treatment of immigrants one of their top issues, while 59% said the same about creating legal status for undocumented immigrants with U.S.-citizen family members. 76% preferred a candidate position calling for a bipartisan path to permanent legal status and immigration reform, compared with 24% who preferred a deportation-focused position. More than 70% in every state surveyed also backed strengthening border security while providing work permits to long-term undocumented immigrants who work and pass a background check. Zoom in: Some of the sharpest divides now run within generations. Among California Latino registered voters under 30, a new UCLA Latino Policy & Politics Institute analysis of UC Berkeley polling found striking differences between men and women. 88% of young Latinas called protecting immigrant communities very important, versus 60% of young Latino men. 82% of young Latinas called fighting President Trump's agenda very important, versus 52% of young Latino men. On defending democracy and protecting voting rights, 92% of young Latinas called the issue very important, versus 74% of young Latino men. Zoom out: In the 2024 presidential election, nearly half of Hispanic voters backed Trump — the best performance by a GOP presidential candidate in modern times, according to an Axios review of past elections dating to 1960. But polls show that advantage has been nearly wiped out as Latinos have turned against Trump's moves on immigration, trade and the economy. A Hart Research-TelevisaUnivision poll this month separately found Democrats ahead 58%-35% among 1,500 Latino registered voters in 17 competitive House districts. What they're saying: "Latino voters are making clear that they don't see border security and legal pathways as competing priorities," Rebecca Shi, executive director of the American Business Immigration Coalition, tells Axios. "Outside the DC bubble, voters aren't one-dimensional: they can want real national security and treating people humanely at the same time," Ashley DeAzevedo, executive director of American Families United, said. The intrigue : A major Latino evangelical group is stepping into the 2026 election conversation with a message about political disagreement and civic responsibility. The National Latino Evangelical Coalition on Friday released "With Love: A Christian Guide to Faithful Voting," a bilingual, nonpartisan guide asking voters to consider three questions about candidates: whether they demonstrate love of neighbor, show trustworthy character and use power responsibly. "Our responsibility to America and to our neighbors continues long after Election Day," NALEC president Rev. Gabriel Salguero said. Methodology: The BSP Research/Shaw & Co. poll is based on a survey conducted Sept. 4-16, 2026 of 1,353 Latino registered voters in seven battleground states: Arizona, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas. The survey was done in English and Spanish through live telephone interviews, text-message invitations and online panels. The overall margin of error is ±2.7 percentage points.
